0.title: That You May Know: The Epistle of Assurance
0.overview:
There is a letter in the New Testament that reads like the heartbeat of an old man who has seen everything and lost nothing. John — the apostle whom Jesus loved, the one who leaned against the Lord at the Last Supper, the one who stood at the foot of the cross when the others had fled (John 13:23; 19:26) — writes at the end of a long life with the urgency of a man who knows that what he carries is the most important thing in the world. He has handled the Word of Life with his own hands. He has seen the glory. And he cannot be silent.

The First Epistle of John was written to a community under assault — not from Rome, but from within. Teachers had arisen who denied the full humanity of Christ, claiming that the eternal Son had not truly come in the flesh, that the spiritual and the material could not really meet. They were sophisticated, confident, and wrong. When they left the fellowship, John writes to those who remain, not to condemn the departed but to assure the faithful: you are not the ones who have missed it. The letter is saturated with the word "know" — used over thirty times. John wants his readers to know that they have eternal life, that they are in fellowship with the Father and the Son, that the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

But assurance in John is never cheap. It is tested by three great evidences that run through the letter like interwoven cords: the moral test (do you walk in the light, keeping his commandments?), the social test (do you love your brothers and sisters?), and the doctrinal test (do you confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh?). These are not conditions for salvation but symptoms of it — the fingerprints of new birth on a redeemed life. The person who has truly been born of God will love, will obey, and will confess. Not perfectly — John is the one who tells us that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves — but genuinely and persistently.

At the theological centre of the letter stands the cross. "The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin" (1:7). "He is the propitiation for our sins" (2:2). "He laid down his life for us" (3:16). "God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (4:10). John circles back to the atoning death of Christ again and again, because the cross is the ground of everything — fellowship, forgiveness, assurance, love. The love of God is not an abstraction in 1 John; it is a specific act: the sending of the Son into the world to bear the wrath that our sins deserved so that we might live through him.

1 John was written to produce settled, humble, joyful assurance in the hearts of those who have truly come to Christ — and such assurance, far from producing complacency, is the very fire that fuels a life of love.

1.title: The Word of Life and the God of Light
1.text: <sup>1</sup>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—<sup>2</sup>the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—<sup>3</sup>that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.<sup>4</sup>And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.<sup>5</sup>This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.<sup>6</sup>If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.<sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.<sup>8</sup>If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.<sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.<sup>10</sup>If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1.overview:
The letter opens with a declaration, not a greeting. John insists four times on the physical reality of what he witnessed: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. The eternal Word became someone John could hold. Against teachers who claimed a higher spiritual knowledge and despised the body, John’s answer is the incarnation.

The purpose is fellowship with the Father, the Son and one another. Then comes the first test: God is light, with no darkness at all. Any claim to know him that is comfortable with sin is self-deception. But the answer to sin is not despair. The blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin, and God forgives all who confess.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any command or warning, John rests the whole letter on one fact: the eternal Word became audible, visible and touchable. John is writing as a man who was there, who ate with him and touched him after he rose. And the purpose of his witness is not just correct information, but that his readers would share the fellowship he has with the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Incarnation as the Ground of Fellowship

The eternal life was heard, seen and touched. A Christ who did not truly come in the flesh could not truly atone, and fellowship with God rests on that fact.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Teachers were spiritualising Christ out of his humanity.

Now: The gospel is not a philosophy but a report of what was heard and seen.

verseByVerse.quote: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—
verseByVerse.commentary:
That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—

Meaning first. 1 John 1 lays the foundation of the letter: the reality of Christ and the reality of fellowship with God. John begins with eyewitness testimony: the eternal Word of life, who was with the Father from the beginning, became visible; the apostles heard him, saw him, and touched him (vv. 1–2). They proclaim him so that the readers can share their fellowship, which is fellowship with the Father and the Son, and so that their joy may be complete (vv. 3–4). The message they heard from him is that God is light, with no darkness at all (v. 5). This exposes three false claims. To claim fellowship with God while walking in darkness is a lie; but walking in the light brings fellowship with one another, and Jesus’ blood cleanses us from all sin (vv. 6–7). To claim to have no sin is self-deception; but if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us (vv. 8–9). To claim we have not sinned makes God a liar (v. 10).

Setting and background. The letter does not name its author, but its language is so close to John’s Gospel that the church has always received it as the work of the apostle John, son of Zebedee, the beloved disciple. He probably wrote from Ephesus near the end of the first century, as an old man (“little children,” 2:1), to churches in Asia. A group had left the church (2:19) teaching a false view of Christ: perhaps an early form of Gnosticism or Docetism, which held that matter is evil and that the divine Christ only seemed to have a human body, or that the divine Christ came on the man Jesus at his baptism and left before his death (Cerinthus, according to Irenaeus). They also claimed to have special knowledge of God while living carelessly and without love. John writes to assure true believers (5:13) and give them tests of genuine faith: truth about Christ, obedience, and love.

That which was from the beginning. Key words. “From the beginning” (ap’ archēs), echoing John 1:1 (“In the beginning was the Word”) and Genesis 1:1. The eternal Son, who existed before creation. John uses the neuter “that which” to embrace the whole message about Christ, his person and work.

Which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands. Key words. Three senses, rising in intensity: heard (akēkoamen), seen (heōrakamen), touched (epsēlaphēsan, handled, felt). “Looked upon” (etheasametha, gazed at, contemplated): not a glance but a long, careful look. John is answering those who denied Jesus had a real body. He and the other apostles touched him, before and after the resurrection (Luke 24:39; John 20:27). The eternal Son became truly, physically human.

Concerning the word of life. Key words. “Word of life” (tou logou tēs zōēs): Christ himself, the Word (John 1:1, 14), who is and gives life (John 1:4; 11:25; 14:6). Also the message about him.

The life was made manifest, and we have seen it. Key words. “Made manifest” (ephanerōthē, was revealed, made visible). The incarnation. Eternal life was invisible; in Jesus it became visible.

And testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life. Key words. “Testify” (martyroumen, bear witness). “Proclaim” (apangellomen, announce). The apostles are witnesses in a court, giving firsthand evidence.

Which was with the Father and was made manifest to us. Key words. “With the Father” (pros ton patera, face to face with the Father), the same phrase as John 1:1 (“the Word was with God”). The Son eternally existed in personal relationship with the Father. He is distinct from the Father, yet eternal and divine.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christianity rests only on the apostles’ experience. It rests on Christ himself; the apostles were eyewitnesses who testified to him. Their testimony is preserved in Scripture.

In a sentence. We proclaim to you what was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked at and our hands have touched: this we proclaim concerning the Word of life. The life appeared; we have seen it and testify to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and has appeared to us.

For worship. Thank God that eternal life became flesh, that the apostles touched him, and that through their testimony you can know him.
verseByVerse.note: The letter does not name its author, but its language is so close to John’s Gospel that it has long been received as the apostle John’s, written late in the first century, probably from Ephesus. Some had left the church denying that Jesus the Christ truly came in the flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.

That which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you. Key words. The main verb of the long sentence (vv. 1–3): “we proclaim.” The apostles pass on what they witnessed.

So that you too may have fellowship with us. Key words. “Fellowship” (koinōnian, sharing, partnership, communion, having something in common). The purpose of proclamation: to bring hearers into the same fellowship the apostles enjoy. Christian fellowship is not merely friendship but sharing a common life in Christ.

And indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. Key words. “Indeed” (kai de, and truly). The apostolic fellowship is not merely human; it is fellowship with God himself, the Father and the Son. Fellowship with God and fellowship with other believers go together. You cannot have one without the other (v. 7). The Father and the Son are named together as equal partners in this fellowship.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fellowship with God depends on the apostles personally. It means the way into fellowship with God is through receiving the apostolic message about Christ. Those who reject the apostolic gospel, as the false teachers did, have no fellowship with God (2:22–23).

In a sentence. We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ.

For worship. Thank God that through the apostles’ message you share fellowship with the Father and the Son, and with all believers.

verseByVerse.quote: And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.

And we are writing these things. Key words. “Writing” (graphomen): the letter is part of the proclamation.

So that our joy may be complete. Key words. “Our joy”: some manuscripts read “your joy.” “Our” is better supported, and it includes both writer and readers. “Complete” (peplērōmenē, filled up, made full). The apostles’ joy is full when others share their fellowship with God. Jesus spoke of the same full joy (John 15:11; 16:24; 17:13). The deepest joy comes from fellowship with God shared with others (3 John 4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christian joy depends on circumstances. It depends on fellowship with God, which nothing can take away.

In a sentence. We write this to make our joy complete.

For worship. Ask God to fill your joy today through fellowship with him and with his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — God Is Light: Walking in the Truth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first thing John says about God is not a comfort but a blinding claim: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” Then he exposes three things people say to live comfortably without facing that light: that they have fellowship with God while walking in darkness, that they have no sin, and that they have not sinned. But the light that exposes also heals. The blood of Jesus cleanses, and God forgives those who confess.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Light

Three claims keep people from the light: fellowship while walking in darkness, having no sin, never having sinned. The remedy is confession to a God who is faithful and just to forgive.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers claimed an enlightenment that placed them above sin.

Now: Honest confession, not self-defence, keeps a believer in fellowship with God.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.

This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you. Key words. “Message” (angelia, announcement). “From him”: from Jesus. The apostles do not invent; they pass on what they received.

That God is light. Key words. “Light” (phōs). In Scripture, light represents God’s holiness, purity, truth, and glory (Psalm 27:1; 36:9; Isaiah 60:19–20; 1 Timothy 6:16). Light reveals, exposes, purifies, gives life. God is not merely a source of light; he is light in his very nature. Jesus is the light of the world (John 8:12).

And in him is no darkness at all. Key words. “No darkness at all” (skotia ouk estin oudemia, a strong double negative: darkness is not in him, none). Darkness represents sin, falsehood, evil, ignorance. God is absolutely holy: no shadow of sin, no mixture of good and evil, no hidden corners (James 1:17). This was aimed at the false teachers, who apparently treated sin as unimportant or claimed that knowledge of God was compatible with sinful living.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is an impersonal force or physical light. It is a metaphor for his moral and spiritual perfection. God is personal.

In a sentence. This is the message we have heard from him and declare to you: God is light; in him there is no darkness at all.

For worship. Worship the God who is pure light. Ask him to shine into every dark corner of your heart.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.

If we say we have fellowship with him. Key words. The first of three false claims, each beginning “If we say” (vv. 6, 8, 10). Perhaps quoting the false teachers’ slogans. “Say” (eipōmen): a claim, not necessarily reality.

While we walk in darkness. Key words. “Walk” (peripatōmen, live, conduct oneself habitually). “In darkness”: living in sin, falsehood, moral evil. A settled way of life, not an occasional failure.

We lie and do not practice the truth. Key words. “Lie” (pseudometha). “Practice the truth” (poioumen tēn alētheian, do the truth): truth is not just something to believe but something to do (John 3:21). If God is light, those who have fellowship with him must walk in light. Claiming fellowship while living in sin is a lie, in word and in life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean any sin in a believer proves he is not a Christian. Verses 8–10 show that believers do sin. It means a settled pattern of living in darkness contradicts a claim to know God.

In a sentence. If we claim to have fellowship with him and yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not live out the truth.

On a Tuesday. Is there an area of your life you keep in the dark? Bring it into God’s light this week.

verseByVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.

But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light. Key words. “Walk in the light”: living openly before God, honestly, in truth and obedience, hiding nothing, letting his light expose and correct us. Not sinlessness, but transparency and obedience. As he is in the light: God dwells in light (1 Timothy 6:16); we walk where he is.

We have fellowship with one another. Key words. Surprising: we might expect “fellowship with him,” but John says “with one another.” Walking in God’s light produces genuine fellowship among believers, because darkness (pretence, hidden sin, hypocrisy) destroys relationships. Fellowship with God and with one another go together (v. 3).

And the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. Key words. “Blood”: Christ’s sacrificial death (Hebrews 9:14, 22; 1 Peter 1:18–19). “Jesus his Son”: the human Jesus is the divine Son, against the false teachers who separated them. His real blood was shed. “Cleanses” (katharizei, purifies, present tense: keeps on cleansing). Not that we are re-justified, but that the ongoing sins of believers are continually covered by Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice. “All sin” (pasēs hamartias): every kind, no exceptions. Walking in the light does not mean we never sin; it means our sins are brought into the light, where Christ’s blood deals with them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s blood must be re-applied through repeated sacrifices or rituals. His sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). Its cleansing power is ongoing.

In a sentence. But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, keeps purifying us from all sin.

For worship. Thank Jesus that his blood keeps cleansing you from all sin. Walk in his light today without fear.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

If we say we have no sin. Key words. The second false claim. “Have no sin” (hamartian ouk echomen): either a claim to a sinless nature (sin is no longer in us) or a claim that sin does not matter, does not count, or is not really sin for the enlightened. The false teachers may have claimed that their special knowledge put them beyond sin, or that what the body does does not affect the spirit.

We deceive ourselves. Key words. “Deceive” (planōmen, lead astray, mislead). We fool ourselves, though we may not fool others.

And the truth is not in us. Key words. To deny our sin is to have no grasp of the truth about God or ourselves. The gospel begins with acknowledging our sin.

Where Christians differ: can a Christian reach sinless perfection in this life? Some Wesleyan and holiness traditions teach that believers can attain entire sanctification, a state free from known sin. Verdict: John says plainly that anyone who says “we have no sin” deceives himself. He includes himself (“we”). Believers are freed from sin’s dominion (3:9; Romans 6:14), and they grow in holiness, but sin remains in them until glory (Romans 7:14–25; James 3:2; Philippians 3:12). We should strive for holiness while daily confessing sin and trusting Christ’s blood.

What it does not mean. It does not excuse sin or make it inevitable in every moment. John writes so that we may not sin (2:1). But when we do, we must not deny it.

In a sentence. If we claim to be without sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.

For worship. Be honest with God today about your sin. Self-deception keeps you from grace; honesty opens the door.

verseByVerse.quote: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

If we confess our sins. Key words. “Confess” (homologōmen, say the same thing, agree, acknowledge). To confess is to agree with God about our sin: to call it what he calls it, without excuse or minimising. Present tense: keep confessing. Specific, honest admission (Psalm 32:5; 51:3–4; Proverbs 28:13).

He is faithful. Key words. “Faithful” (pistos, reliable, trustworthy). God keeps his promises. He has promised to forgive those who confess (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:12).

And just. Key words. “Just” (dikaios, righteous). Surprising: we might expect “merciful.” But forgiveness is just because Christ has paid for sin (2:2; Romans 3:25–26). God would be unjust to punish twice for the same sin. Because Christ’s blood has satisfied justice, God’s justice now guarantees forgiveness for those who are in Christ.

To forgive us our sins. Key words. “Forgive” (aphē, release, send away, cancel the debt).

And to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. Key words. “Cleanse” (katharisē, purify), as in verse 7. Forgiveness removes guilt; cleansing removes defilement. Both are complete: “all unrighteousness.”

Where Christians differ: must we confess to a priest to be forgiven? Roman Catholic teaching requires confession of serious sins to a priest. Verdict: John directs confession to God (“he is faithful and just to forgive”). Christ is our only mediator and advocate (2:1; 1 Timothy 2:5). Confessing sins to one another is good and healing (James 5:16), but forgiveness comes directly from God through Christ, not through priestly absolution.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers lose their justification when they sin and regain it when they confess. Justification is once for all (Romans 8:1). Confession restores the enjoyment of fellowship with God, like a child confessing to a father, not a criminal before a judge. Nor does it mean unconfessed sins are unforgiven in the judicial sense; it means confession is how believers continually live in the experience of forgiveness.

In a sentence. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.

For worship. Confess your sins to God specifically today. Then believe his promise: he has forgiven and cleansed you.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.

If we say we have not sinned. Key words. The third false claim. “Have not sinned” (ouch hēmartēkamen, perfect tense: we have not sinned and are in a sinless state). A denial of ever having sinned, or of having sinned since conversion. Even worse than verse 8.

We make him a liar. Key words. God has declared that all have sinned (Romans 3:23; Psalm 14:3; Isaiah 53:6). He sent his Son to die for sin. To deny our sin is to call God a liar and to make the cross unnecessary.

And his word is not in us. Key words. “His word”: his revealed truth, Scripture, the gospel. Its message has not penetrated our hearts. Someone who claims never to have sinned has never really heard God’s word.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should dwell morbidly on our sins. John writes to bring assurance and joy (v. 4; 5:13). Honest confession leads to forgiveness and freedom.

In a sentence. If we claim we have not sinned, we make him out to be a liar and his word is not in us.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you have been calling something else: a mistake, a weakness, a personality trait? Call it sin, confess it, and receive forgiveness.

1.theology:
The Incarnation as Foundation. Everything in 1 John rests on the physical, historical, tangible reality of the incarnation. John's stacked verbs in verses 1–2 — heard, seen, looked upon, touched — are a theological rampart against every form of docetism (the heresy that Christ only appeared to be human). If Christ did not truly come in flesh, the blood shed on Calvary has no atoning value, the resurrection is a spirit's trick, and there is no real fellowship between God and humanity. The incarnation is not incidental to Christianity; it is its structural foundation. God became graspable so that we could grasp him — and through him, life.

The God Who is Light. John's declaration that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" has massive ethical implications. Fellowship with a God of absolute moral purity cannot coexist with a comfortable relationship with sin. The light of God is not a comfortable mood but a searching, penetrating, all-revealing reality. It is also a liberating one: in the light, where our sin is exposed, the blood of Jesus cleanses. Reformed theology has always insisted on the holiness of God as the backdrop against which the grace of God becomes luminous. You cannot appreciate the gospel without first standing in the light of who God is.
1.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had just experienced a painful split. People they had worshipped with, broken bread with, called brothers and sisters, had walked out. The departure of the false teachers left wounds and questions. Were the ones who stayed the ones who had missed the deeper truth? John's answer in chapter 1 is the apostolic testimony: we were there. We heard him, saw him, touched him. This is not speculation; it is witness. The assurance of the community rests not on their spiritual experiences but on the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses of the Word of Life.

Now: We live in a culture that treats the interior life as the truest life — feelings, impressions, spiritual experiences. The incarnation is John's counter-word: Christianity is tethered to history, to flesh, to blood, to an empty tomb. Our fellowship with God is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the historical reality of the Son of God made flesh. And the practice of confession — agreeing with God about what we are — is the daily discipline that keeps that fellowship living and real. Every day we come back to the same place: not to earn forgiveness, but to receive what has already been purchased.

2.title: Our Advocate, Our Obedience, Our Love
2.text: <sup>1</sup>My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.<sup>2</sup>He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.<sup>3</sup>And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.<sup>4</sup>Whoever says “I know him” but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him,<sup>5</sup>but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:<sup>6</sup>whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.<sup>8</sup>At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.<sup>9</sup>Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.<sup>10</sup>Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.<sup>11</sup>But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.<sup>12</sup>I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.<sup>13</sup>I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.<sup>14</sup>I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.<sup>15</sup>Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.<sup>16</sup>For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.<sup>17</sup>And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.<sup>18</sup>Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.<sup>19</sup>They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.<sup>20</sup>But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.<sup>21</sup>I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.<sup>22</sup>Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.<sup>23</sup>No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.<sup>24</sup>Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.<sup>25</sup>And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.<sup>26</sup>I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.<sup>27</sup>But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.<sup>28</sup>And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.<sup>29</sup>If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
2.overview: Chapter 2 moves in three steps. First, John wants his readers not to sin, but knows they will, and points them to their advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins. Second, he gives the first test of real faith: obedience. Not sinless perfection, but a life that keeps God’s commands and walks as Jesus walked, and that loves the brothers. Third, he warns against loving the world, which is passing away, and against the antichrists who have left the church, and he urges his readers to abide in what they heard from the beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Advocate and the Test of Knowing God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John aims at holiness: he writes so that his people will not sin. But he knows they will, so the provision comes with the command. We have an advocate with the Father, who pleads not our innocence but his own righteousness, and who is himself the propitiation that turned away God’s wrath. On that ground of grace, John gives the first test: those who know him keep his commandments and walk as he walked.
verseByVerse.theology:
Advocate and Propitiation

John writes so that believers will not sin, and provides for when they do: Jesus Christ the righteous pleads for us, and he is the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Separating the divine Christ from the suffering Jesus emptied the cross.

Now: Knowing God shows itself in keeping his commandments and walking as Jesus walked.

verseByVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.

Meaning first. 1 John 2 gives tests by which believers may know that they truly know God, and warns against the world and false teachers. John writes so that his children will not sin; but if they do, they have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the propitiation for their sins and for the whole world (vv. 1–2). The first test is obedience: those who know God keep his commands and walk as Jesus walked (vv. 3–6). The second is love: the old and yet new command to love; whoever hates his brother is still in darkness (vv. 7–11). John then assures his readers, children, fathers and young men, that their sins are forgiven, they know the Father, and they have overcome the evil one (vv. 12–14). So they must not love the world, with its desires and pride, which is passing away; whoever does God’s will lives forever (vv. 15–17). It is the last hour; many antichrists have come, people who left the church because they never really belonged, who deny that Jesus is the Christ, and so deny both the Father and the Son (vv. 18–23). But the readers have the Spirit’s anointing and know the truth; they must let the original message remain in them and remain in Christ, so that they may be confident when he appears (vv. 24–29).

My little children. Key words. “Little children” (teknia, dear children), a tender term used seven times in the letter. An aged apostle speaking as a spiritual father.

I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. Key words. “May not sin” (hina mē hamartēte, aorist: may not commit an act of sin). Chapter 1 might be misused: if everyone sins and God forgives, why worry? John answers: the goal is not to sin. Forgiveness is not a licence.

But if anyone does sin. Key words. “If” (ean): John knows believers will sin (1:8, 10).

We have an advocate with the Father. Key words. “Advocate” is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit (“Helper,” John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7). Paraklētos: one called alongside to help, especially a defence lawyer in court. The Spirit is our advocate within us; Christ is our advocate before the Father. When Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), Christ speaks for us. “With the Father” (pros ton patera, face to face with the Father), as in 1:2. Our advocate is in the Judge’s presence and is the Judge’s Son.

Jesus Christ the righteous. Key words. “The righteous” (dikaion): Christ is perfectly righteous. His plea is not that we are innocent, but that he has paid for our sins (v. 2). An advocate who is himself righteous can plead for the guilty on the basis of his own righteousness.

What it does not mean. Christ’s advocacy does not mean the Father is reluctant and must be persuaded. The Father sent the Son in love (4:9–10). Christ’s advocacy is his continual presence before the Father as the one whose sacrifice covers our sins (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34).

In a sentence. My dear children, I write this to you so that you will not sin. But if anybody does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the Righteous One.

For worship. When you sin today, do not hide or despair. Turn to Jesus, your advocate, who stands before the Father for you.
verseByVerse.note: “Advocate” is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit (“Helper”) in John’s Gospel; here it is Jesus himself pleading for us.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.

He is the propitiation for our sins. Key words. “He is” (autos estin, he himself is): not merely he provided, but he himself is the propitiation. A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. “Propitiation” (hilasmos, atoning sacrifice, the means of appeasing wrath). The word is related to the mercy seat in the tabernacle (Hebrews 9:5). Christ’s death satisfied God’s just wrath against sin by bearing it in our place (Romans 3:25; Hebrews 2:17; 1 John 4:10). This is why the Father can be both just and forgiving (1:9). Penal substitution.

And not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. Key words. “Ours”: John and his readers, Jewish and Gentile believers. “The whole world” (holou tou kosmou). This is a key verse in debates about the extent of the atonement.

Where Christians differ: did Christ propitiate the sins of every person? Arminians and others read “the whole world” as every individual without exception, so that Christ’s death was a propitiation for the sins of all people, including those who are finally lost. Universalists conclude that all will be saved. Verdict: Propitiation means God’s wrath is actually turned away. If Christ propitiated God’s wrath for every individual, then no one would face God’s wrath, which Scripture denies (John 3:36; Revelation 14:10). So “the whole world” must mean something other than every individual. In John’s writings, “world” often means people of every kind and nation, not just Jews (John 11:51–52, where Caiaphas prophesied that Jesus would die “for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad”). John’s point is that Christ’s sacrifice is not limited to one group, John’s churches, or Jewish believers; it is for people throughout the whole world, of every nation (Revelation 5:9). It is also the only propitiation there is: there is no other sacrifice available anywhere in the world. This is definite atonement: Christ’s death actually and effectively propitiated God for all his people, from every nation. Its value is infinite and sufficient for all, and the gospel is offered sincerely to all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean John is restricting the gospel invitation. The gospel is to be preached to every person, and anyone who believes will be saved (John 3:16). It means the propitiation is effective, not merely potential.

In a sentence. He is the atoning sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath from our sins, and not only from ours but from the sins of people throughout the whole world.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he bore God’s wrath for your sins. Pray for people of every nation who still need to hear of this sacrifice.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath.

verseByVerse.quote: And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.

And by this we know that we have come to know him. Key words. “Know” (ginōskomen), a keyword of 1 John, used about forty times. “Have come to know” (egnōkamen, perfect tense: have known and continue to know). The false teachers claimed special knowledge of God; John gives tests by which true knowledge can be recognised. “By this” (en toutō): a phrase John uses repeatedly to introduce tests.

If we keep his commandments. Key words. “Keep” (tērōmen, observe, guard, obey, present tense: habitually keep). “His commandments”: God’s moral will, summed up in love for God and neighbour (3:23; John 13:34; 15:12). The first test: obedience. Knowing God is not merely intellectual; it shows itself in a changed life (John 14:15, 21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn knowledge of God by obedience, or that perfect obedience is required. John has said we all sin (1:8). It means a settled pattern of obedience is evidence that we truly know God.

In a sentence. We know that we have come to know him if we keep his commands.

On a Tuesday. Look at your life this week: where is there clear evidence of obedience to Christ? Thank God for it, and ask for growth where there is little.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:

Whoever says I know him. Key words. Another false claim, as in 1:6, 8, 10. Perhaps the false teachers’ slogan.

But does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. Key words. “Liar” (pseustēs). Strong language. A claim to know God without obedience is false. The truth has not taken hold of him.

But whoever keeps his word. Key words. “His word” (autou ton logon): broader than “commandments,” the whole of God’s revealed will.

In him truly the love of God is perfected. Key words. “Love of God” (hē agapē tou theou): God’s love for us, or our love for God, or the love that comes from God. Probably our love for God, which shows itself in obedience (5:3; John 14:15). “Perfected” (teteleiōtai, brought to completion, reached its goal). Love for God reaches its full expression in obedience.

By this we may know that we are in him. Key words. “In him” (en autō): union with Christ. Another test, leading into verse 6.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love for God is only a matter of obedience, with no feeling. It means genuine love always shows itself in obedience.

In a sentence. Whoever says, “I know him,” but does not do what he commands is a liar, and the truth is not in that person. But if anyone obeys his word, love for God is truly made complete in them. This is how we know we are in him:

On a Tuesday. Do your words about knowing God match your life? Ask God to make your obedience as real as your profession.

verseByVerse.quote: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.

Whoever says he abides in him. Key words. “Abides” (menein, remains, stays, dwells, continues). A favourite word of John (John 15:4–10). To abide in Christ is to live in continuing union and fellowship with him.

Ought to walk in the same way in which he walked. Key words. “Ought” (opheilei, is obligated, owes it). “Walk” (peripatein, live). “He” (ekeinos, that one): Jesus, emphatically. The test is Christlikeness: living as Jesus lived, in love, obedience, humility and holiness (John 13:15; 1 Peter 2:21). Jesus’ earthly life is the pattern.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must imitate every detail of Jesus’ life (being a carpenter, staying unmarried, walking on water). It means we must follow his character and pattern of obedience to the Father and love for others.

In a sentence. Whoever claims to live in him must live as Jesus did.

On a Tuesday. Pick one encounter in Jesus’ life from the Gospels. How can you walk as he walked in a situation this week?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — The Old-New Commandment: Love and Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The command to love is both old and new. Old, because it was there from the beginning (Leviticus 19:18). New, because Christ has given it a new measure, “as I have loved you” (John 13:34), and because the new age has begun: the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining. The test of whether we are in the light is concrete: do we love our brother?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Old-New Commandment

The command to love is old, and new in Christ, because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The split in the church showed where the darkness was.

Now: Nursed grudges blind; love keeps the path clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.

Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment. Key words. “Beloved” (agapētoi). John is not introducing novel teaching, unlike the false teachers.

But an old commandment that you had from the beginning. Key words. “Old” (palaian). “From the beginning”: from when they first heard the gospel. The command to love, taught by Jesus and passed on by the apostles. Its roots go back to the Old Testament (Leviticus 19:18).

The old commandment is the word that you have heard. Key words. Part of the original apostolic message.

What it does not mean. It does not mean John’s teaching was merely traditional. It was apostolic, and he will show how it is also new (v. 8).

In a sentence. Dear friends, I am not writing you a new command but an old one, which you have had since the beginning. This old command is the message you have heard.

For worship. Thank God for the old, unchanging truth of the gospel. You do not need something new; you need to live the old.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.

At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you. Key words. “New” (kainēn, new in quality, fresh). Jesus called it “a new commandment” (John 13:34): love one another as I have loved you. It is old in its source (from the beginning) but new in its standard (Christ’s love) and its power (the new age).

Which is true in him and in you. Key words. “True” (alēthes, real, realised). The command is fulfilled in Christ’s life, and is being fulfilled in believers.

Because the darkness is passing away. Key words. “Passing away” (paragetai, is going by, disappearing, present tense). The old age of sin and darkness is ending.

And the true light is already shining. Key words. “True light” (to phōs to alēthinon): Christ (John 1:9; 8:12). “Already” (ēdē). The new age has dawned with Christ’s coming. Light and darkness overlap now, but the darkness is fading.

What it does not mean. It does not mean darkness has vanished completely. The world still lies in the evil one’s power (5:19). But the dawn has come, and the day is certain.

In a sentence. Yet I am writing you a new command; its truth is seen in him and in you, because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

For worship. Praise Christ, the true light, who is already shining. Ask him to drive the darkness from your life.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.

Whoever says he is in the light. Key words. Another claim, as in verses 4 and 6.

And hates his brother. Key words. “Hates” (misōn, present tense: keeps on hating). Hatred includes contempt, resentment, ill will, refusing to love. “His brother”: a fellow member of the church. The false teachers apparently despised ordinary believers.

Is still in darkness. Key words. “Still” (heōs arti, until now). Whatever he claims, he has never left the darkness. The second test: love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer can never feel anger or have conflict with another believer. It describes a settled attitude of hatred and contempt.

In a sentence. Anyone who claims to be in the light but hates a brother or sister is still in the darkness.

On a Tuesday. Is there a believer you resent or despise? Ask God to replace that with love, and take one step toward reconciliation.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.

Whoever loves his brother abides in the light. Key words. “Loves” (agapōn, present tense: keeps on loving). Love shows that one is in the light.

And in him there is no cause for stumbling. Key words. “Cause for stumbling” (skandalon, trap, snare, stumbling block). Either: the loving person does not stumble himself (he can see where he is going), or: he does not cause others to stumble. Probably both. Love keeps us from tripping and from tripping others (Romans 14:13; Psalm 119:165).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the loving person never sins. It means love keeps him on the path.

In a sentence. Anyone who loves their brother and sister lives in the light, and there is nothing in them to make them stumble.

For worship. Thank God for those who love you and keep you from stumbling. Ask him to make you that kind of person for others.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness. Key words. “Is in” and “walks in”: his position and his practice. He lives in darkness.

And does not know where he is going. Key words. Like someone stumbling in the dark, without direction (John 12:35).

Because the darkness has blinded his eyes. Key words. “Blinded” (etyphlōsen). Hatred is not only a sin; it blinds. A person full of hatred cannot see clearly about God, himself, or others (2 Corinthians 4:4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean such a person cannot be rescued. Christ came to open blind eyes (John 9:39). But hatred must be repented of.

In a sentence. But anyone who hates a brother or sister is in the darkness and walks around in the darkness. They do not know where they are going, because the darkness has blinded them.

On a Tuesday. Has resentment been blinding you to the truth about someone? Ask God to open your eyes and help you see them as he does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Assurance for Every Stage of Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the tests, John pauses to reassure. He addresses little children, fathers and young men, and tells each what is already theirs: forgiveness, knowledge of the eternal Christ, and victory over the evil one through the word abiding in them. Assurance comes before further commands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance for Every Stage

Before further commands, John tells children, fathers and young men what is already theirs: forgiveness, knowledge of God, and victory over the evil one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were being told they needed something more.

Now: The newest believer needs first to hear that his sins are forgiven for Christ’s name’s sake.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.

I am writing to you, little children. Key words. After hard tests, John pauses to reassure. Verses 12–14 address three groups: “little children,” “fathers,” and “young men.” Either these are three stages of spiritual maturity, or “little children” addresses all believers (as in v. 1), and “fathers” and “young men” are two groups within the church, older and younger.

Because your sins are forgiven. Key words. “Because” (hoti): either “because” (the reason for writing) or “that” (the content). Probably “because”: John writes to them because they are genuine believers. “Are forgiven” (apheōntai, perfect tense: have been forgiven and remain forgiven). Forgiveness is the foundation of everything. Every believer, from the youngest, is fully forgiven.

For his name’s sake. Key words. “His name”: Christ’s name, his person and work (Acts 4:12; 10:43). Forgiveness is on account of who Christ is and what he has done, not on account of anything in us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean forgiveness is conditional on passing all the tests. The tests show who is forgiven; they do not earn forgiveness.

In a sentence. I am writing to you, dear children, because your sins have been forgiven on account of his name.

For worship. Rest in this today: your sins are forgiven, completely and permanently, for Christ’s sake.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.

I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. Key words. “Fathers”: mature believers, perhaps older in years. “Him who is from the beginning”: Christ, the eternal Word (1:1). The mark of maturity: a deep, long-tested knowledge of Christ. Not new ideas, but deepening intimacy with the eternal one.

I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. Key words. “Young men”: believers in the vigour of spiritual life, perhaps younger in years. “Overcome” (nenikēkate, perfect tense: have conquered and remain victorious). “The evil one”: Satan (5:18–19). Young believers are in the thick of battle, and they have won by Christ’s victory (4:4; 5:4–5; John 16:33).

I write to you, children, because you know the Father. Key words. “Children” (paidia, little ones, young children), a different word from verse 12. The simplest and most precious knowledge: knowing God as Father (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean each group has only one quality. All believers are forgiven, know the Father, overcome the evil one, and grow in knowing Christ. Each is highlighted in its characteristic stage.

In a sentence. I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, dear children, because you know the Father.

For worship. Whatever stage you are at, thank God: you know the Father, you can overcome the evil one, and you can grow to know Christ more deeply.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.

I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. Key words. Repeated from verse 13 for emphasis. The tense changes from “I am writing” to “I write” (egrapsa, aorist), perhaps referring to the whole letter, or to an earlier writing, or simply for variety and emphasis.

I write to you, young men, because you are strong. Key words. “Strong” (ischyroi). Spiritual strength.

And the word of God abides in you. Key words. The source of their strength: God’s word dwelling in them (John 15:7; Colossians 3:16; Psalm 119:11). Jesus overcame Satan in the wilderness by quoting Scripture (Matthew 4:1–11).

And you have overcome the evil one. Key words. Strength through the word leads to victory over Satan (Ephesians 6:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean young believers never struggle with temptation. They are in the fight. But they fight from victory, with the word as their weapon.

In a sentence. I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God lives in you, and you have overcome the evil one.

On a Tuesday. Memorise one verse of Scripture this week. Let God’s word abide in you as your weapon against the evil one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — Do Not Love the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “Do not love the world.” John does not mean God’s creation, which God loves, or a call to withdraw from culture. He means the world system organised against God, with its own values and desires. He names its three roots: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life. And he gives the decisive reason: the world is passing away, but whoever does God’s will abides for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
Do Not Love the World

The desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life are not from the Father. The world is passing away; whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Wealth and religion were on public display in the cities of Asia.

Now: Receive created things as gifts, but enthrone none of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.

Do not love the world. Key words. “Love” (agapate, present tense: keep on loving, make it your settled affection). “The world” (ton kosmon): not the created earth (which is good, Genesis 1:31) or the people of the world (whom God loves, John 3:16), but human society organised apart from and against God, with its values, desires and priorities (James 4:4; 5:19).

Or the things in the world. Key words. The things it values and offers: possessions, pleasures, status, power, when sought as ends in themselves, in place of God.

If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. Key words. “Love of the Father”: love for the Father. Love for the world and love for God are mutually exclusive as ultimate loyalties (Matthew 6:24; James 4:4). You cannot love both supremely.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should withdraw from society, despise beauty, or refuse to enjoy God’s good gifts (1 Timothy 4:4; 6:17). It means they must not give their hearts to the world’s rebellious system or let its values rule them.

In a sentence. Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, love for the Father is not in them.

On a Tuesday. What does the world offer that most tempts your heart? Name it, and give your heart to the Father instead.

verseByVerse.quote: For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.

For all that is in the world. Key words. Three things sum up the world’s system.

The desires of the flesh. Key words. “Desires” (epithymia, cravings, lusts). “Flesh” (sarkos): sinful human nature. Cravings for physical gratification: sexual immorality, gluttony, drunkenness, laziness, comfort above all.

And the desires of the eyes. Key words. Cravings aroused by what we see: covetousness, greed, envy, materialism, pornography. The eyes lead the heart (Genesis 3:6; Joshua 7:21; 2 Samuel 11:2).

And pride of life. Key words. “Pride” (alazoneia, arrogance, boastful pretension, showing off), as in James 4:16. “Life” (biou, livelihood, possessions, means of living). Arrogance about what one has or does: status, wealth, achievements, appearance. The same three appeared in Eve’s temptation: the fruit was good for food (flesh), a delight to the eyes (eyes), and desirable to make one wise (pride) (Genesis 3:6). And in Jesus’ temptation: bread (flesh), the kingdoms of the world (eyes), throwing himself from the temple (pride) (Luke 4:1–13).

Is not from the Father but is from the world. Key words. These desires do not come from God. They come from the fallen world system.

What it does not mean. It does not mean physical desires, beauty or achievements are sinful in themselves. God made our bodies, our eyes and our abilities. The problem is desire that is disordered, ruling us in place of God.

In a sentence. For everything in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, comes not from the Father but from the world.

For worship. Ask God to show you which of these three has the strongest grip on you, and pray for freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.

And the world is passing away along with its desires. Key words. “Passing away” (paragetai, going by, disappearing, present tense), as in verse 8. The world’s system, with all its attractions, is temporary and already fading (1 Corinthians 7:31). Why love what you will lose?

But whoever does the will of God abides forever. Key words. Does the will of God: lives in obedience (Matthew 7:21; 12:50). “Abides forever” (menei eis ton aiōna, remains to the age, endures eternally). Not that obedience earns eternal life, but that those who do God’s will share in his eternal life and will last when the world is gone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the world will be annihilated. The present order will be renewed (2 Peter 3:13). What passes away is the world as a rebellious system.

In a sentence. The world and its desires pass away, but whoever does the will of God lives for ever.

On a Tuesday. Invest this week in what lasts: God’s will, God’s word, God’s people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Antichrists, Apostasy, and the Anointing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Antichrists have appeared and left the church, denying the Father and the Son. John turns this crisis into confidence. Their departure revealed that they never truly belonged. And ordinary believers have what the false teachers claimed and lacked: the anointing of the Holy Spirit, who teaches them the truth and keeps them in it. The answer to deception is to abide in what was heard from the beginning, and so in the Son and the Father.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Anointing

Those who left showed that they were never of the church. Every believer has the anointing of the Spirit, who keeps him in the truth he heard from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers offered superior knowledge.

Now: Beware any teaching that says Scripture, the Spirit and the church are not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.

Children, it is the last hour. Key words. “Children” (paidia), as in verse 14. “Last hour” (eschatē hōra): the final period of history before Christ’s return, which began with his first coming (Hebrews 1:2; 1 Peter 1:20). The whole church age is “the last hour,” the final stage of God’s plan.

And as you have heard that antichrist is coming. Key words. “Antichrist” appears in the Bible only in John’s letters (2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7). “Anti” (anti) means against, or in place of: one who opposes Christ, or who sets himself up as a false Christ. The readers had been taught that a great opponent of Christ would come at the end, as Jesus and Paul foretold (Mark 13:22; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–12, the man of lawlessness; Revelation 13, the beast).

So now many antichrists have come. Key words. “Many” (polloi). Before the final antichrist, many smaller antichrists appear: all who deny Christ, especially false teachers within the church (vv. 19, 22). The spirit of antichrist is already at work (4:3).

Therefore we know that it is the last hour. Key words. Their presence is evidence that the final period has begun.

Where Christians differ: who is the antichrist? Some identify the antichrist with a specific future world ruler who will appear during a seven-year tribulation after a secret rapture; the Reformers often identified the papacy as the antichrist; others see the antichrist as a principle only, not a person. Verdict: John teaches both: the spirit of antichrist is present throughout the church age in the many who deny Christ, and Scripture also foretells a final, personal climax of opposition before Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8). This fits the amillennial view: throughout the age between Christ’s comings, antichrists arise, culminating in a final great deceiver whom Christ will destroy at his single, visible return. Believers should not speculate about identities but test every spirit by its confession of Christ (4:1–3).

What it does not mean. “Last hour” does not mean John expected the end within months. It describes the character of the age. Nor should believers be fearful; antichrists cannot snatch Christ’s sheep (John 10:28).

In a sentence. Dear children, this is the last hour; and as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have come. This is how we know it is the last hour.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear about Jesus this week: does it confess him truly as the Christ, God come in the flesh?
verseByVerse.note: “Antichrist” appears in the Bible only in John’s letters.

verseByVerse.quote: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.

They went out from us. Key words. The false teachers had left the church, perhaps forming a rival group. “From us” (ex hēmōn): they had been members, part of the fellowship.

But they were not of us. Key words. “Of us” (ex hēmōn): truly belonging, sharing the same life. They were among us, but not of us. Their membership was outward only.

For if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. Key words. “Continued” (memenēkeisan, would have remained, abided). True believers persevere. Those who are genuinely born of God continue in the faith and the fellowship.

But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us. Key words. “Become plain” (phanerōthōsin, be revealed, be made manifest). Their departure exposed what was always true: they never truly belonged. God used their leaving to reveal their real condition.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer fall away and be lost? Verdict: This verse is one of the clearest statements of the perseverance of the saints. Those who finally depart from Christ and his people show that they were never truly “of us,” never genuinely regenerated. If they had been, “they would have continued.” True believers may stumble, backslide and need restoring, but they will not finally fall away, because God keeps them (John 6:37–40; 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). This is not a cause for complacency, but for assurance, and for testing ourselves.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone who leaves a particular church is an unbeliever. People move, churches err, and believers sometimes leave for good reasons. John speaks of those who left the apostolic faith and fellowship, denying Christ (v. 22).

In a sentence. They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us; but their going showed that none of them belonged to us.

For worship. Thank God that he keeps his own to the end. Pray for those who have drifted away, that they may truly come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.

But you have been anointed by the Holy One. Key words. “But you”: in contrast with those who left. “Anointed” (chrisma echete, you have an anointing). “Chrisma” is related to “Christ” (Christos, Anointed One) and “antichrist.” The antichrists lack the anointing; believers have it. The anointing is the Holy Spirit, given to all believers (2 Corinthians 1:21–22; Acts 10:38). “The Holy One”: Christ (John 6:69; Acts 3:14), who gives the Spirit (John 15:26; 16:7), or God the Father.

And you all have knowledge. Key words. “You all” (pantes). Some manuscripts read “you know all things” (panta). “You all” is better supported. Against the false teachers who claimed knowledge only for an elite, John says every believer has the Spirit and knows the truth (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every believer knows everything. It means every believer has the Spirit, who enables them to recognise the truth of the gospel and to discern error.

In a sentence. But you have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth.

For worship. Thank God for the anointing of the Spirit, who lives in you and helps you know the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.

I write to you, not because you do not know the truth. Key words. John is not adding new knowledge.

But because you know it. Key words. He writes to confirm and strengthen what they already know.

And because no lie is of the truth. Key words. “Of the truth” (ek tēs alētheias, comes from the truth). Truth and lies have different sources. Because they know the truth, they can recognise lies (John 8:44; 14:6). Truth is not relative; there is a clear line between truth and falsehood.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are immune to deception. John warns them (v. 26). It means they have what they need to resist it.

In a sentence. I do not write to you because you do not know the truth, but because you do know it and because no lie comes from the truth.

On a Tuesday. Strengthen what you already know: review the core truths of the gospel this week, so you can recognise lies.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.

Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? Key words. “The liar” (ho pseustēs, the liar par excellence). “Denies that Jesus is the Christ”: the false teachers apparently separated the human Jesus from the divine Christ, claiming the Christ-spirit came on Jesus at his baptism and left before his death (the view associated with Cerinthus). To deny that Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah, the eternal Son come in the flesh (4:2), is the ultimate lie.

This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son. Key words. “The antichrist”: the embodiment of the antichrist spirit (v. 18). “Denies the Father and the Son”: you cannot deny the Son without denying the Father, because the Father is known only through the Son (John 14:6–9). Claims to know God while rejecting Jesus as the Christ are false.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone with a confused view of Jesus is the antichrist. John speaks of a deliberate denial of the apostolic truth about Christ, by those who once knew it.

In a sentence. Who is the liar? It is whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ. Such a person is the antichrist, denying the Father and the Son.

For worship. Confess today with joy that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God come in the flesh. Through him you know the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.

No one who denies the Son has the Father. Key words. “Has” (echei): possesses, in relationship with. There is no access to the Father apart from the Son. All other religions, however sincere, which deny the Son, do not have the Father (John 5:23; 14:6; Acts 4:12). This is Christian exclusivism.

Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also. Key words. “Confesses” (homologōn, acknowledges publicly). Confessing the Son brings the Father with him. Father and Son are inseparable.

Where Christians differ: can people be saved through other religions? Inclusivists hold that people of other faiths may be saved through Christ without knowing him; pluralists that all religions lead to God. Verdict: John’s statement is absolute: no one who denies the Son has the Father. Salvation is found in Christ alone, received through faith in him (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17). This is why the church must take the gospel to every nation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should be arrogant toward people of other religions. It means they must lovingly point them to the only Saviour.

In a sentence. No one who denies the Son has the Father; whoever acknowledges the Son has the Father also.

On a Tuesday. Pray for a friend of another faith or no faith, that they will come to know the Father through the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.

Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. Key words. “What you heard from the beginning”: the original apostolic gospel. Not new teaching (v. 7). “Abide” (menetō, remain, stay). Hold onto the original message; do not drift to novelties.

If what you heard from the beginning abides in you. Key words. The condition: keep the truth.

Then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father. Key words. Holding the apostolic truth keeps us in union with God. Truth and fellowship with God go together (John 8:31; 15:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we keep ourselves saved by holding onto doctrine through our own strength. God keeps us (5:18), through his word abiding in us.

In a sentence. As for you, see that what you have heard from the beginning remains in you. If it does, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father.

For worship. Thank God for the original gospel you heard. Ask him to keep it living in you, and you in him.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.

And this is the promise that he made to us. Key words. “Promise” (epangelia). “He”: Christ.

Eternal life. Key words. “Eternal life” (tēn zōēn tēn aiōnion): not merely endless existence, but the life of God himself, knowing the Father and the Son (John 17:3), now and forever (5:11–13; John 10:28). The reward of abiding in the Son is eternal life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eternal life is only future. Believers have it now (5:12–13). It will be fully experienced at Christ’s return.

In a sentence. And this is what he promised us: eternal life.

For worship. Thank Christ for his promise of eternal life, which you already possess and will enjoy forever.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.

I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you. Key words. “Trying to deceive” (planōntōn, leading astray, present tense: they are actively trying). The false teachers were still at work, trying to win over those who remained.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the readers had been deceived. John writes to protect them before they are.

In a sentence. I am writing these things to you about those who are trying to lead you astray.

On a Tuesday. Be alert to anyone trying to lead you away from the truth about Christ, whether in person, in books or online.

verseByVerse.quote: But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.

But the anointing that you received from him abides in you. Key words. “Anointing” (chrisma): the Holy Spirit, as in verse 20. “Abides”: the Spirit remains permanently (John 14:16–17).

And you have no need that anyone should teach you. Key words. A striking statement. In context, John means: you do not need the false teachers, with their claims to new, higher knowledge. You already have the Spirit and the apostolic truth. You do not need anything beyond what you received from the beginning.
