But as his anointing teaches you about everything. Key words. “Teaches” (didaskei). The Spirit teaches believers, guiding them into the truth (John 14:26; 16:13), not by giving new revelation, but by illuminating the apostolic word, confirming it in their hearts, and enabling them to discern error.

And is true, and is no lie. Key words. The Spirit is the Spirit of truth (John 14:17).

Just as it has taught you, abide in him. Key words. “Abide in him”: in Christ. The Spirit’s teaching always leads to Christ.

Where Christians differ: does this verse mean believers do not need teachers? Some have used this verse to reject all church teaching, or to claim private revelations from the Spirit. Verdict: John himself is teaching them in this very letter. Christ gave teachers to the church (Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 2:2). John means they do not need the false teachers’ new “knowledge,” because the Spirit has given them the true knowledge through the apostolic gospel. The Spirit does not give new revelation that contradicts or adds to Scripture; he illuminates Scripture and confirms its truth to the heart. Every claim to Spirit-given teaching must be tested by the apostolic word (4:1–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should be independent of the church or of faithful teachers. It means they are not dependent on human teachers in the way the false teachers claimed, as if the Spirit were not enough.

In a sentence. As for you, the anointing you received from him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things, and as that anointing is real, not counterfeit, just as it has taught you, remain in him.

For worship. Thank God for the Spirit who teaches you through his word. Ask him to illuminate Scripture as you read it today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — Abide in Him: The Returning King and the Family Likeness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by looking to Christ’s return. John urges his dear children to remain in Christ now, so that when he appears they will meet him with confidence instead of shrinking from him in shame at his coming. Then he introduces a theme that will run through the rest of the letter: because God is righteous, everyone who practises righteousness shows the family likeness of one who has been born of him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Abide in him

Abide in Christ so as to have confidence at his coming. Those born of the righteous God practise righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Christ’s appearing was still ahead.

Now: Live now as someone who will meet him face to face.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.

And now, little children, abide in him. Key words. “Abide” (menete, keep remaining). The command that sums up the chapter.

So that when he appears. Key words. “Appears” (phanerōthē, is revealed, made visible). Christ’s second coming, visible and public.

We may have confidence. Key words. “Confidence” (parrēsian, boldness, freedom of speech, openness). Like a child running to greet a returning father, not hiding.

And not shrink from him in shame at his coming. Key words. “Shrink in shame” (aischynthōmen, be put to shame, shrink back ashamed). Those who have not abided in him will be ashamed. “Coming” (parousia, arrival, presence): the only use of this word in John’s writings.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be condemned if they are not perfect. It means those who abide in Christ will meet him with joyful confidence, not guilty fear.

In a sentence. And now, dear children, continue in him, so that when he appears we may be confident and unashamed before him at his coming.

For worship. Abide in Christ today, so that you can look forward to his coming with confidence and joy.

verseByVerse.quote: If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.

If you know that he is righteous. Key words. “He”: Christ (v. 1) or God the Father (since “born of him” refers to the Father). “Righteous” (dikaios).

You may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him. Key words. “Practices righteousness” (poiōn tēn dikaiosynēn, does righteousness, present tense: habitually). “Has been born of him” (ex autou gegennētai, perfect tense: has been begotten and remains so). The first mention of new birth in 1 John. Note the order: being born of God comes first; practising righteousness follows as the evidence. Not that doing right causes new birth, but that new birth produces doing right. Children resemble their Father. This is the test of righteousness, introducing chapter 3.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only the perfectly righteous are born again. It means a settled pattern of righteous living shows that one is God’s child.

In a sentence. If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who does what is right has been born of him.

For worship. Thank God for giving you new birth. Ask him to make you more like your Father in righteousness.

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The paired terms of 2:1–2 give us the two aspects of Christ's saving work seen from different angles. As advocate, he represents us before the Father — our case is in his hands, and he is qualified to plead it because he is righteous. As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation — the wrath of God against our sin has been absorbed at the cross. These are not two separate acts but two perspectives on the one act of the cross. The same sacrifice that satisfied divine justice now grounds our ongoing access to divine mercy. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is both objective (propitiation — something accomplished outside us, in history, on a cross) and applied (advocacy — an ongoing ministry of Christ on our behalf). Both are necessary; together they produce the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John's three tests — obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11), and belief (2:22–23) — are not a checklist for earning assurance but symptoms of new birth. Just as a doctor looks for signs of life, John looks for the signs that genuine regeneration has occurred. These tests are not meant to produce anxiety but clarity: not "have I been good enough?" but "is there genuine fruit of the Spirit in my life?" The tests are cumulative and mutually reinforcing — genuine obedience produces love; genuine love flows from right belief; genuine belief manifests in how we treat the brothers and sisters.
2.examples:
Then: The antichrists who had left the community had claimed a superior knowledge of God. Their departure seemed, to some, like the enlightened ones leaving the unenlightened behind. John's response is pastoral and pointed: the ones who left proved by their leaving that they were never truly of the community (2:19). This is not cruelty but theology — genuine new birth produces perseverance. The ones who remained, confused and perhaps diminished, were the ones who had "the anointing from the Holy One" and knew the truth (2:20). The test of authenticity is not sophistication but faithfulness to the beginning.

Now: We live in a world of novelty — new spiritualities, new therapies, new paths to self-actualization. The church is perpetually tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more culturally current, more psychologically satisfying, more intellectually respectable. John's word is the same: let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. The gospel does not need to be updated; it needs to be inhabited. The depth we seek is not found by moving beyond the cross — it is found by going deeper into it.

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.<sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.<sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.<sup>4</sup>Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.<sup>5</sup>You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.<sup>6</sup>No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.<sup>7</sup>Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.<sup>8</sup>Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.<sup>9</sup>No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.<sup>10</sup>By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.<sup>11</sup>For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.<sup>12</sup>We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.<sup>13</sup>Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.<sup>14</sup>We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.<sup>15</sup>Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.<sup>16</sup>By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.<sup>17</sup>But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?<sup>18</sup>Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.<sup>19</sup>By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him;<sup>20</sup>for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.<sup>21</sup>Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;<sup>22</sup>and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.<sup>23</sup>And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.<sup>24</sup>Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens in wonder: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are.” We are God’s children now, and when Christ appears we shall be like him. That hope makes us pure.

Then John shows what God’s children look like. They do not live in sin, because God’s seed abides in them and the Son came to destroy the devil’s works. And they love one another, not in words only, but in deeds, as Christ laid down his life for us. When the heart condemns, God is greater than our heart. His command is to believe in his Son and love one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Children of God: Now and Not Yet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John commands us to look: “See what kind of love”. The phrase suggests something foreign and astonishing. God calls us his children, “and so we are”. The world does not recognise us, because it did not recognise him. We are children now; what we will be is not yet seen. But when Christ appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. And everyone with that hope purifies himself now.
verseByVerse.theology:
Children Now, Like Him Then

We are God’s children now; when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. That hope purifies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some claimed they had already arrived.

Now: We become what we behold; set your hope on his appearing.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.

Meaning first. 1 John 3 is about the children of God: who they are, how they live, and how they can be sure. It opens in wonder at the Father’s love that makes us his children, now, though what we will be is not yet revealed; when Christ appears we will be like him, and this hope purifies us (vv. 1–3). Then the test of righteousness: sin is lawlessness; Christ came to take away sins and destroy the devil’s works; so no one born of God keeps on sinning as a settled practice, because God’s seed remains in him; the children of God and the children of the devil are distinguished by whether they practise righteousness and love (vv. 4–10). Then the test of love: from the beginning the message has been to love one another, not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother; the world will hate us, but love for the brothers proves we have passed from death to life; hatred is murder in the heart (vv. 11–15). True love is defined by Christ laying down his life for us, and so we ought to lay down our lives for one another, including practical help for a brother in need; love in deed and truth, not just words (vv. 16–18). By this we can reassure our hearts before God even when they condemn us, for God is greater than our hearts; with a clear heart we have confidence in prayer, keeping his command to believe in his Son and love one another; and we know he abides in us by the Spirit he has given us (vv. 19–24).

See what kind of love the Father has given to us. Key words. “See” (idete, behold, look!): an exclamation of wonder. “What kind of” (potapēn, what sort of, from what country, how foreign and astonishing). A love from another world, utterly unlike human love. “Given” (dedōken, perfect tense: has given and it remains). Love as a gift.

That we should be called children of God. Key words. “Called” (klēthōmen): named, given the title. “Children” (tekna, born ones). Not merely adopted (though that is true, Romans 8:15), but born of God (2:29), sharing his nature.

And so we are. Key words. “And so we are” (kai esmen, and we are!). Not just a title, but a reality. Some later manuscripts omit it; the earliest include it. We are truly God’s children, now.

The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him. Key words. “The world”: unbelieving humanity. “Does not know”: does not recognise, understand or accept. The world did not recognise Jesus as the Son of God (John 1:10–11); so it does not recognise his children. Our true identity is hidden from the world, as his was.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all people are God’s children by nature. All are his creatures, but only those born of him by faith in Christ are his children (John 1:12–13; 8:42–44).

In a sentence. See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are! The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know him.

For worship. Stop and marvel at this: you are God’s child. Thank the Father for his astonishing love.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

Beloved, we are God’s children now. Key words. “Now” (nyn): present reality, not merely future hope.

And what we will be has not yet appeared. Key words. “Not yet appeared” (oupō ephanerōthē, not yet been revealed). Our final state is not yet visible. We are children now, but the full glory of what that means is hidden (Romans 8:18–19; Colossians 3:3–4).

But we know that when he appears we shall be like him. Key words. “When he appears” (ean phanerōthē): Christ’s return (2:28). “Like him” (homoioi autō): like Christ in his glorified humanity: holy, immortal, with resurrection bodies (Philippians 3:21; 1 Corinthians 15:49; Romans 8:29). Not divine in essence, but conformed to his image.

Because we shall see him as he is. Key words. “See him as he is” (opsometha auton kathōs estin). The beatific vision. Now we see dimly (1 Corinthians 13:12); then face to face (Revelation 22:4; Matthew 5:8). Seeing him will transform us. As Moses’ face shone after seeing God’s glory (Exodus 34:29), so seeing Christ fully will make us fully like him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become God or lose our individual identity. It means we will be perfected in his likeness.

In a sentence. Dear friends, now we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet been made known. But we know that when Christ appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.

For worship. Long for the day you will see Christ as he is. Let that hope fill your heart today.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.

And everyone who thus hopes in him. Key words. “Hopes” (echōn tēn elpida, has this hope). “In him” (ep’ autō, set on him): hope fixed on Christ.

Purifies himself as he is pure. Key words. “Purifies” (hagnizei, makes holy, cleanses, present tense: keeps purifying). The word used of ritual purification before a festival (John 11:55). Hope of seeing Christ leads to preparing for that meeting. “As he is pure” (hagnos): Christ is the standard. Eschatology produces ethics: true hope in Christ’s return always leads to holy living (2 Peter 3:11–14; Titus 2:12–13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we purify ourselves by our own power. Christ’s blood cleanses (1:7), and the Spirit sanctifies. But we actively cooperate, turning from sin and pursuing holiness (2 Corinthians 7:1).

In a sentence. All who have this hope in him keep purifying themselves, just as he is pure.

On a Tuesday. If Christ came today, what would you want to have dealt with? Deal with it now, as one preparing to see him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Sin, the Devil, and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This passage must be read carefully, or it will either terrify the true believer or comfort the false one. John speaks of two families, known by how they live. The devil has sinned from the beginning; the Son of God appeared to destroy his works. God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives. John is not teaching sinless perfection (1:8–10), but that the new birth changes the direction of a life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Birth

The Son appeared to take away sins and to destroy the works of the devil. God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Claimed spiritual knowledge was being used to excuse sin.

Now: Avoid both errors: tolerating sin as normal, and thinking that any sin proves you are not born again.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.

Everyone who makes a practice of sinning. Key words. “Makes a practice of sinning” (ho poiōn tēn hamartian, the one doing sin, present tense: habitually, as a way of life). The contrast with “practices righteousness” (2:29).

Also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness. Key words. “Lawlessness” (anomia, rebellion against God’s law, defiance). Sin is not a mere mistake or weakness; it is rebellion against God himself. The false teachers may have treated sin as trivial; John defines it as defiance of God. “Lawlessness” also has end-time overtones: the “man of lawlessness” (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Persistent sin aligns a person with the antichrist.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every sin a believer commits is deliberate rebellion. But all sin, at root, is a departure from God’s will.

In a sentence. Everyone who sins breaks the law; in fact, sin is lawlessness.

For worship. Ask God to help you see sin as he sees it: not trivial, but rebellion against him. Then thank him for forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.

You know that he appeared in order to take away sins. Key words. “Appeared” (ephanerōthē, was revealed): his incarnation. “Take away” (arē, lift up, carry away, remove), as in John 1:29: “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” Christ came to remove sin: its guilt by his death, its power by his Spirit. To continue in sin contradicts the very purpose of his coming.

And in him there is no sin. Key words. Christ is sinless (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). The sinless one came to remove sin. Those united to him cannot be at home in sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ removed all sin from believers instantly. He removed its guilt completely and is removing its presence progressively, and will remove it entirely at his return (v. 2).

In a sentence. But you know that he appeared so that he might take away our sins. And in him is no sin.

For worship. Thank Jesus, the sinless Lamb, who came to take away your sins.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.

No one who abides in him keeps on sinning. Key words. The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse. “Keeps on sinning” (hamartanei, present tense: continually sins, sins as a pattern of life). Those living in union with Christ do not live in persistent, unrepented sin.

No one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him. Key words. “Has seen” (heōraken, perfect tense) and “known” (egnōken, perfect tense). Spiritual seeing and knowing. Someone who lives a life of habitual sin has never truly encountered Christ. True knowledge of Christ transforms.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a true believer never sins. John has said that would be self-deception (1:8–10), and he has provided for believers who sin (2:1–2). The present tense indicates ongoing, characteristic practice. A believer may fall into sin, even serious sin, but will not remain comfortable in it as a way of life.

In a sentence. No one who lives in him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has either seen him or known him.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you have settled into as a habit? Union with Christ calls you out of it. Confess it and ask for his power to change.
verseByVerse.note: The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse (compare 1:8–2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.

Little children, let no one deceive you. Key words. “Deceive” (planatō, lead astray). The false teachers taught that one could be righteous without living righteously.

Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous. Key words. “Practices righteousness” (ho poiōn tēn dikaiosynēn, habitually does what is right). “Is righteous” (dikaios estin). The one who habitually does right shows that he is righteous, like Christ. Not that doing right makes him righteous (justification is by faith alone), but that doing right reveals the reality of a righteous standing and a renewed nature (2:29).

What it does not mean. It does not mean our righteous deeds are the basis of our righteousness before God. Christ’s righteousness credited to us is the basis (Philippians 3:9). Our deeds are the evidence.

In a sentence. Dear children, do not let anyone lead you astray. The one who does what is right is righteous, just as he is righteous.

For worship. Thank God for Christ’s righteousness credited to you, and ask him to make your life reflect it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.

Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil. Key words. “Of the devil” (ek tou diabolou, from the devil, belonging to him). Not that he is literally born of the devil, but that he shares the devil’s character and belongs to his family (John 8:44).

For the devil has been sinning from the beginning. Key words. “From the beginning” (ap’ archēs): from the beginning of his rebellion, or from the beginning of human history (Genesis 3). Sin is the devil’s nature.

The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil. Key words. “Destroy” (lysē, loosen, undo, dismantle, break up). “Works of the devil”: sin, deception, death, bondage. Christ came to undo all of it (Hebrews 2:14; Colossians 2:15; Genesis 3:15). He has already won the decisive victory at the cross, and will complete it at his return.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers who sin belong to the devil. Habitual, unrepentant sin as a way of life reveals the devil’s family. Believers who sin and repent belong to God.

In a sentence. The one who keeps on sinning is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the devil’s work.

For worship. Praise the Son of God who came to destroy the devil’s works. Ask him to destroy those works in your life.

verseByVerse.quote: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.

No one born of God makes a practice of sinning. Key words. “Born of God” (ho gegennēmenos ek tou theou, perfect tense: has been born and remains so). “Makes a practice of sinning” (hamartian ou poiei, does not do sin habitually).

For God’s seed abides in him. Key words. “Seed” (sperma): God’s life implanted in the believer at the new birth, his nature (2 Peter 1:4), the Holy Spirit, or the word of God (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18). Probably the divine life itself, given through the word by the Spirit. “Abides” (menei, remains permanently). It does not die or leave.

And he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God. Key words. “Cannot” (ou dynatai, is not able). “Keep on sinning” (hamartanein, present infinitive: continue sinning as a lifestyle). The new nature makes persistent, comfortable sin impossible. A child of God cannot settle down in sin, because God’s life in him resists it. This is also a promise of perseverance: the seed remains.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach sinless perfection? Some read “cannot sin” as teaching that a born-again person is incapable of sinning at all, or that sinless perfection is possible. Verdict: John has already said that anyone who claims to be sinless is deceived (1:8, 10), and he provides for believers who sin (2:1). The present tense verbs in chapter 3 indicate habitual practice. A child of God cannot continue in a settled lifestyle of unrepented sin, because God’s seed in him makes it impossible. He may fall, but he will not stay down. He will be grieved, convicted and restored. This is the Reformed doctrine of perseverance and progressive sanctification.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never sin, or that a single sin proves one is not born of God. It means sin is no longer the believer’s master or his comfortable habitat (Romans 6:14).

In a sentence. No one who is born of God will continue to sin, because God’s seed remains in them; they cannot go on sinning, because they have been born of God.

For worship. Thank God that his seed remains in you, and that he will not let you settle in sin. Rest in his keeping power.

verseByVerse.quote: By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.

By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil. Key words. “Evident” (phanera, visible, manifest, plain). There are only two families. Every person belongs to one or the other (John 8:42–47). The difference shows in how they live.

Whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God. Key words. The test of righteousness (vv. 4–10).

Nor is the one who does not love his brother. Key words. The test of love, introduced here and developed in verses 11–18. Righteousness and love go together. Love is the heart of righteousness (Romans 13:8–10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can always tell with certainty who is a child of God by outward observation. God alone knows the heart. But the general pattern of a life reveals its family.

In a sentence. This is how we know who the children of God are and who the children of the devil are: anyone who does not do what is right is not God’s child, nor is anyone who does not love their brother and sister.

On a Tuesday. Which family does your life resemble this week? Ask God to make your righteousness and love unmistakable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — Love One Another: The Cain Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John brings love down to earth: the brother in front of you. He starts with Cain, who hated and murdered his brother because Abel was righteous. That is why the world hates believers. Then comes the clearest definition of love in the New Testament: “By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us.” The cross defines love, and obliges us to love the same way, starting with an open hand to a brother in need.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love Defined by the Cross

Cain hated his brother; Christ laid down his life for us. By this we know love, and we ought to lay down our lives for one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The world’s hatred was not to surprise the church.

Now: Love in deed and truth: an open hand to a brother in need.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.

For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning. Key words. “Message” (angelia), as in 1:5. The first message was “God is light”; the second, “love one another.” “From the beginning”: from the first preaching of the gospel (2:7).

That we should love one another. Key words. “Love” (agapōmen, keep loving). Jesus’ new commandment (John 13:34–35; 15:12, 17). Love for fellow believers is not optional but central to the Christian faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love only for believers. Christians love all people, even enemies (Matthew 5:44). But love for the family of God is a special mark of belonging to it.

In a sentence. For this is the message you heard from the beginning: we should love one another.

For worship. Thank God for the believers he has given you to love. Pray for one of them by name today.

verseByVerse.quote: We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.

We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one. Key words. Cain is the first example of hatred in Scripture (Genesis 4:1–16). “Of the evil one” (ek tou ponērou, from the evil one): he belonged to the devil’s family (v. 10).

And murdered his brother. Key words. “Murdered” (esphaxen, slaughtered, butchered, cut the throat, a word used of slaughtering sacrificial animals). A brutal word for a brutal act.

And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous. Key words. Cain was not provoked by Abel’s wrongdoing, but by his righteousness. God accepted Abel’s offering, which exposed Cain’s evil heart (Genesis 4:4–7; Hebrews 11:4). Evil hates good because good exposes it (John 3:19–20). This explains why the world hates believers (v. 13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every conflict between believers is like Cain and Abel. But it warns that hatred begins with envy and resentment, and can end in murder.

In a sentence. Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own actions were evil and his brother’s were righteous.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone whose goodness makes you resentful? Confess it, and pray for them instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.

Do not be surprised, brothers. Key words. “Surprised” (thaumazete, amazed, astonished), as in 1 Peter 4:12.

That the world hates you. Key words. “Hates” (misei, present tense: keeps on hating). As Cain hated Abel, the world hates the righteous. Jesus warned of it (John 15:18–20; 17:14). The world’s hatred is evidence that believers belong to Christ, not to it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every unbeliever hates every believer, or that Christians should be offensive. It means opposition from the world is normal, not strange.

In a sentence. Do not be surprised, my brothers and sisters, if the world hates you.

For worship. If the world hates you for Christ’s sake, take heart: it hated him first. You belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.

We know that we have passed out of death into life. Key words. “Passed” (metabebēkamen, crossed over, moved from one place to another, perfect tense: have passed and remain). Echoing Jesus: whoever hears and believes “has passed from death to life” (John 5:24). Conversion is a transfer from spiritual death to spiritual life (Ephesians 2:1–5).

Because we love the brothers. Key words. “Because” (hoti): love is the evidence, not the cause. We know we have passed into life because love for fellow believers has appeared in us. Love is the sign of new life.

Whoever does not love abides in death. Key words. “Abides in death” (menei en tō thanatō, remains in death). Without love, there is no evidence of new life. Such a person is still spiritually dead.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are saved by loving. We are saved by grace through faith in Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9). Love is the fruit and the proof.

In a sentence. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love each other. Anyone who does not love remains in death.

For worship. Thank God for the love for his people he has put in your heart. It is a sign that you have passed from death to life.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.

Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. Key words. “Murderer” (anthrōpoktonos, man-killer), the word Jesus used of the devil (John 8:44). Hatred is murder in the heart, the root from which murder grows. Jesus taught the same: anger and contempt make one liable to judgement (Matthew 5:21–22). God judges the heart, not just the act.

And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him. Key words. Eternal life and settled hatred cannot coexist. A heart ruled by hatred shows no evidence of eternal life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a murderer cannot be saved. Paul was complicit in murder (Acts 8:1; 22:20) and was forgiven. It means that a person who lives in unrepented hatred does not have eternal life. Repentance and faith bring forgiveness for any sin.

In a sentence. Anyone who hates a brother or sister is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life residing in them.

On a Tuesday. Take hatred seriously: it is murder in the heart. If you harbour it, bring it to the cross today.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.

By this we know love. Key words. “Know” (egnōkamen, have come to know). The supreme definition of love is not a feeling or a theory, but an event: the cross.

That he laid down his life for us. Key words. “He” (ekeinos, that one): Jesus. “Laid down” (ethēken, placed, set aside), the phrase Jesus used of the Good Shepherd (John 10:11, 15, 17–18). Voluntary, deliberate self-giving. “For us” (hyper hēmōn, on our behalf, in our place): substitution. Christ died the death we deserved.

And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. Key words. “Ought” (opheilomen, owe, are obligated). The love Christ showed is the pattern for our love. Not that our deaths atone, but that we should be willing to sacrifice everything, even life itself, for fellow believers (John 15:12–13). Usually this means daily, practical self-giving (v. 17); sometimes it means literal death, as with martyrs.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our sacrifice has any saving value. Only Christ’s death atones. It means his love, which saved us, now shapes how we love others.

In a sentence. This is how we know what love is: Jesus Christ laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters.

For worship. Gaze at the cross today: this is what love is. Then ask God how you can give yourself for someone else this week.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?

But if anyone has the world’s goods. Key words. “The world’s goods” (ton bion tou kosmou, the life of the world, livelihood, means of living, possessions). John moves from the dramatic (laying down life) to the everyday (sharing goods). Many will never be asked to die for others, but all are asked to share.

And sees his brother in need. Key words. “Sees” (theōrē, observes, looks at, contemplates). Not a passing glance, but a clear awareness of the need. “In need” (chreian echonta, having need).

Yet closes his heart against him. Key words. “Closes his heart” (kleisē ta splanchna autou ap’ autou, shuts his inward parts, his compassion, against him). A deliberate refusal of compassion.

How does God’s love abide in him? Key words. “God’s love”: love for God, or the love that comes from God. A rhetorical question: it does not. Love that refuses to help is not God’s love (James 2:15–16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must give to every request without wisdom (2 Thessalonians 3:10). It means we must not harden our hearts against genuine need when we have the means to help.

In a sentence. If anyone has material possessions and sees a brother or sister in need but has no pity on them, how can the love of God be in that person?

On a Tuesday. Is there a fellow believer in need whom you could help this week? Open your heart and your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.

Little children, let us not love in word or talk. Key words. “Word” (logō) and “talk” (glōssē, tongue). Love that is only words: saying “I love you” or “I’ll pray for you” without action.

But in deed and in truth. Key words. “Deed” (ergō, work, action). “Truth” (alētheia, reality, genuineness). Real love acts, and is genuine, not hypocritical.

What it does not mean. It does not mean words of love are worthless. Encouraging words are important (1 Thessalonians 5:11). It means words alone are not enough; love must show itself in action.

In a sentence. Dear children, let us not love with words or speech but with actions and in truth.

On a Tuesday. Turn one of your words of love into a deed this week: a meal, a gift, help with a task, a visit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — Assurance, Prayer, and the Mutual Indwelling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After such a demanding call to love, the question follows: what if I have not loved enough? What if my heart condemns me? John answers tenderly: God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything. Then comes the freedom of prayer, and a summary of the whole Christian life: believe in the name of God’s Son, and love one another. The Spirit he has given assures us that he lives in us.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Greater than Our Heart

When our heart condemns us, God is greater and knows everything. His commandment is to believe in his Son and to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Assurance rested on love in deed and on the Spirit given to them.

Now: A tender conscience can rest in God’s fuller knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.

By this we shall know that we are of the truth. Key words. “By this”: by loving in deed and truth (v. 18). “Of the truth” (ek tēs alētheias, from the truth, belonging to it). Genuine love is evidence that we belong to God.

And reassure our heart before him. Key words. “Reassure” (peisomen, persuade, convince, set at rest). Our hearts sometimes accuse us. In God’s presence, we can quiet them.

For whenever our heart condemns us. Key words. “Condemns” (kataginōskē, knows something against, accuses). A tender conscience, conscious of failure, may accuse and doubt.

God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything. Key words. “Greater” (meizōn). “Knows everything” (ginōskei panta). Two readings: (1) God is greater in mercy: he knows everything, including our genuine love and Christ’s atonement, so we can rest even when our hearts accuse us; or (2) God is greater in judgement: if our hearts condemn us, how much more will God, who knows everything. The context (reassurance, v. 19; confidence, v. 21) supports the first. When an over-sensitive conscience accuses, we appeal to the God who knows all, including our love for him (John 21:17), and who has forgiven us in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should ignore our conscience when it rightly convicts us of sin. We confess and are forgiven (1:9). It means that when our hearts continue to accuse us after confession, God’s verdict outweighs our feelings.

In a sentence. This is how we know that we belong to the truth, and how we set our hearts at rest in his presence: if our hearts condemn us, we know that God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.

For worship. If your heart accuses you today, bring it to God. He knows everything, including that you love him, and he is greater than your heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;

Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us. Key words. When our conscience is at rest, clean through confession and Christ’s blood, and our lives show genuine love.

We have confidence before God. Key words. “Confidence” (parrēsian, boldness, freedom), as in 2:28. Not arrogance, but freedom to approach God as a child approaches a loving father (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean confidence rests on our performance. It rests on Christ. But a clear conscience removes the barriers to enjoying that confidence.

In a sentence. Dear friends, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God

For worship. Come to God today with confidence, as a beloved child, through Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.

And whatever we ask we receive from him. Key words. “Whatever” (ho ean). “Receive” (lambanomen, present tense: keep receiving). A sweeping promise (John 14:13–14; 15:7; 16:23–24). Qualified by 5:14: if we ask according to his will.

Because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him. Key words. “Because” (hoti): not that obedience earns answered prayer, but that obedient children ask according to their Father’s will, and their prayers align with what pleases him (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; James 5:16). A life of obedience and a life of answered prayer go together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God answers every request exactly as we want if we are obedient enough. God answers according to his wisdom and will (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). It means obedient children pray as their Father desires, and their prayers are heard.

In a sentence. and receive from him anything we ask, because we keep his commands and do what pleases him.

On a Tuesday. Bring your requests to God with confidence today, seeking to please him in everything.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.

And this is his commandment. Key words. “Commandment” (entolē, singular). The commandments (v. 22) are summed up in one commandment with two parts.

That we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ. Key words. “Believe” (pisteusōmen, aorist: come to believe, trust). Faith is the first commandment (John 6:29). “In the name” (tō onomati): in his person and character, all he is. “His Son Jesus Christ”: the full confession the false teachers denied (2:22–23). The first mention of believing in 1 John.

And love one another, just as he has commanded us. Key words. “Love” (agapōmen, present tense: keep loving). Faith and love together, the two great tests of the letter. Right belief about Christ and right love for one another are inseparable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith and love are equal grounds of salvation. Faith receives salvation; love flows from it (Galatians 5:6).

In a sentence. And this is his command: to believe in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, and to love one another as he commanded us.

For worship. Renew your faith in Jesus Christ today, and show it by loving someone.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.

Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. Key words. “Abides” (menei): mutual indwelling. The believer lives in God, and God lives in the believer (John 14:23; 15:4–5). The deepest possible union. Obedience is the sign of this union.

And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us. Key words. “By the Spirit”: the first mention of the Holy Spirit by name in 1 John. The Spirit is the guarantee of God’s presence in us (Romans 8:9, 16; 2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13–14). How do we know he is in us? By the Spirit’s work: enabling us to confess Christ (4:2), to love (4:13), and to obey. The Spirit gives inner assurance, and his fruit gives outward evidence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Spirit’s presence is known only by dramatic experiences. The Spirit is known primarily by the fruit he produces: true confession of Christ, love, obedience (Galatians 5:22–23).

In a sentence. The one who keeps God’s commands lives in him, and he in them. And this is how we know that he lives in us: we know it by the Spirit he gave us.

For worship. Thank God for the Holy Spirit he has given you, the guarantee that he lives in you.

3.theology:
Adoption and Transformation. The doctrine of adoption is one of the richest in the New Testament, and 3:1–3, with its language of being born of God and called his children, is one of its highest expressions. To be called children of God is not a metaphor of religious devotion; it is a declaration of a new ontological status. We have been brought into the family of God — not as servants, not as subjects, but as children who share in the inheritance of the Son. And adoption in John is both present reality ("so we are," v.1) and future consummation ("what we will be has not yet appeared," v.2). The "not yet" of our glorification does not undermine the "already" of our adoption; the hope of the appearing purifies the life of the one who holds it.

Love Defined by the Cross. John's definition of love in verse 16 is one of the most consequential sentences in the New Testament. He does not say "God is love, therefore love is whatever feels loving." He says love is defined by a specific act: the laying down of the life of the Son. The cross is love's definition, love's measure, and love's demand. Reformed theology has always insisted that the love of God is not sentimentality but holy self-giving at infinite cost. Every theology of love that avoids the cross will eventually become a theology of tolerance — and tolerance is not love. Love is the cross, and the cross makes demands.
3.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had experienced the pain of betrayal — people they had loved had left. The temptation in such a situation is to turn inward, to protect the heart, to love in word only and keep the real self safely guarded. John's word to them is the cross: he laid down his life. Not as an inspiration to imitate from a safe distance, but as the very definition and pattern of what love is. The ones who remained in the fellowship were called to love one another with an openness that made them vulnerable — precisely because that is what love, defined by the cross, requires.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that defines love primarily as acceptance and validation. John defines it as sacrifice. The question is not "do I feel warmly toward my brother?" but "am I laying anything down for my brother?" The test of love is not interior but behavioural — not word and talk but deed and truth. A closed hand toward a brother in need, whatever feelings accompany it, is not love in John's sense. The cross makes love costly, specific, and concrete.

4.title: Testing the Spirits and the Love of God
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.<sup>2</sup>By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God,<sup>3</sup>and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.<sup>4</sup>Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.<sup>5</sup>They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.<sup>6</sup>We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.<sup>8</sup>Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.<sup>9</sup>In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.<sup>10</sup>In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.<sup>11</sup>Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.<sup>12</sup>No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.<sup>13</sup>By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.<sup>14</sup>And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.<sup>15</sup>Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.<sup>16</sup>So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.<sup>17</sup>By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.<sup>18</sup>There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.<sup>19</sup>We love because he first loved us.<sup>20</sup>If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.<sup>21</sup>And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 begins with a warning and rises to the fullest teaching on the love of God in the New Testament. The warning: test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out. The test is whether a teaching confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Then John says twice, “God is love” (vv. 8, 16). He never lets this become vague. God’s love is defined by its greatest act: he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. That love casts out the fear of punishment, and it flows on through us to one another: “We love because he first loved us.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Testing the Spirits: Discernment in the Last Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits.” Not every teaching that claims to come from God does. False prophets rarely announce themselves; they use Christian words with spiritual intensity. John’s test goes to the heart of the gospel: does the teaching confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? And he ends with confidence: “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing the Spirits

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: False prophets had gone out into the world.

Now: Ask of any teaching whether it confesses the whole Christ — truly God, truly man, crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.

Meaning first. 1 John 4 brings together the two great tests: truth about Christ and love. First, test the spirits (vv. 1–6): many false prophets are in the world, so do not believe every spirit. The test is confession: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; every spirit that denies this is the spirit of antichrist. Believers have overcome these false prophets, because he who is in them is greater than he who is in the world; the world listens to its own, but those who know God listen to the apostles. Second, love (vv. 7–21). Love is from God, for God is love; whoever loves is born of God (vv. 7–8). God showed his love by sending his only Son to give us life and to be the propitiation for our sins; love is not that we loved God but that he loved us (vv. 9–10). So we ought to love one another; though no one has seen God, if we love one another, God abides in us (vv. 11–12). We know we abide in him because he has given us his Spirit, and we confess that the Father sent the Son as Saviour of the world (vv. 13–16). Love perfected gives confidence for the day of judgement, because perfect love casts out fear (vv. 17–18). We love because he first loved us; anyone who claims to love God but hates his brother is a liar; whoever loves God must love his brother (vv. 19–21).

Beloved, do not believe every spirit. Key words. “Spirit” (pneumati): the spirit behind a prophet or teacher. Every teacher speaks under the influence of a spirit: either the Holy Spirit or a spirit of error (v. 6). The church at that time had many who claimed to speak by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3; 14:29). Not every claim is true.

But test the spirits to see whether they are from God. Key words. “Test” (dokimazete, examine, prove, as metal is tested for purity), present tense: keep testing. Believers are not to be gullible. Every teaching, however spiritual it seems, must be tested (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; Acts 17:11).

For many false prophets have gone out into the world. Key words. “False prophets” (pseudoprophētai): the false teachers who had left the church (2:19), claiming to speak for God. Jesus warned of them (Matthew 7:15; 24:11, 24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should be suspicious of all teaching or cynical about every teacher. It means discernment is required, and the standard is apostolic truth about Christ (vv. 2, 6).

In a sentence. Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.

On a Tuesday. Test the next sermon, book or online teaching you encounter. What does it say about Jesus? Does it match Scripture?

verseByVerse.quote: By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.

By this you know the Spirit of God. Key words. The test of the Spirit: what is confessed about Christ.

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. Key words. “Confesses” (homologei, acknowledges, declares publicly). “Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (Iēsoun Christon en sarki elēlythota, perfect tense: has come and remains in the flesh). The incarnation: the eternal Son truly became a real human being, with a real body. The false teachers denied this, claiming the divine Christ only seemed to be human, or that the Christ-spirit came on the man Jesus temporarily (2:22). The Holy Spirit always glorifies Christ and testifies to his true identity (John 15:26; 16:14; 1 Corinthians 12:3).

And every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. Key words. “Does not confess Jesus”: does not acknowledge Jesus as he truly is, the Christ come in the flesh. Some early manuscripts and church fathers read “every spirit that annuls (lyei, dissolves, separates) Jesus,” meaning separates the human Jesus from the divine Christ. The best reading is “does not confess.”

This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already. Key words. The antichrist spirit (2:18, 22) is already active, working through false teachers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who mechanically says “Jesus came in the flesh” is from God. The confession must be genuine, with the full meaning of who Jesus is: God the Son, truly incarnate, the Christ who died and rose. Even demons acknowledged Jesus’ identity (Mark 1:24) without being from God.

In a sentence. This is how you can recognise the Spirit of God: every spirit that acknowledges that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, but every spirit that does not acknowledge Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and even now is already in the world.

For worship. Confess with joy today: Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, has come in the flesh. Worship the incarnate Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.

Little children, you are from God. Key words. “You” (hymeis, emphatic): in contrast with the false prophets. “From God” (ek tou theou, belonging to God, born of him).

And have overcome them. Key words. “Overcome” (nenikēkate, perfect tense: have conquered and remain victorious), as in 2:13–14. “Them”: the false prophets. The readers had resisted their teaching and stayed faithful.

For he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world. Key words. “He who is in you”: God, by his Spirit (3:24). “He who is in the world”: the devil, “the ruler of this world” (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11), working through the false prophets. “Greater” (meizōn). The victory is not because believers are stronger, but because God in them is infinitely greater than Satan. A tremendous comfort.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will never struggle with false teaching or temptation. It means they will ultimately overcome, because God is with them.

In a sentence. You, dear children, are from God and have overcome them, because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.

For worship. Whatever you face today, remember: the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.

They are from the world. Key words. “They”: the false prophets. “From the world” (ek tou kosmou): their source, values and loyalty are worldly.

Therefore they speak from the world. Key words. Their message reflects the world’s thinking: what the world wants to hear, what is fashionable, comfortable and acceptable.

And the world listens to them. Key words. The world welcomes teachers who tell it what it wants to hear (2 Timothy 4:3–4; John 15:19). Popularity with the world is no proof of truth; often it is a warning sign.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everything popular is false, or that faithful teachers will never be heard by unbelievers. Many have come to faith through faithful preaching. It means worldly approval is not the test of truth.

In a sentence. They are from the world and therefore speak from the viewpoint of the world, and the world listens to them.

On a Tuesday. Is a teaching popular because it is true, or because it tells people what they want to hear? Test it by Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.

We are from God. Key words. “We”: John and the apostles, the authoritative witnesses (1:1–3). They are God’s spokesmen.

Whoever knows God listens to us. Key words. “Listens” (akouei, hears, heeds). Those who truly know God recognise and accept the apostolic teaching (John 8:47; 10:27; 18:37). The sheep know the Shepherd’s voice.

Whoever is not from God does not listen to us. Key words. Rejecting the apostles’ teaching reveals that one does not belong to God.

By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error. Key words. “Spirit of truth”: the Holy Spirit (John 14:17; 15:26; 16:13). “Spirit of error” (pneuma tēs planēs, spirit of deception): Satan and his demonic influences. The second test of spirits: do they accept the apostolic witness? Today, the apostolic teaching is preserved in the New Testament. Any teaching that contradicts it comes from the spirit of error.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every church leader today has apostolic authority. “We” refers to the apostles, whose unique authority is now exercised through Scripture. Modern teachers must be tested by the apostolic word, not the other way round.

In a sentence. We are from God, and whoever knows God listens to us; but whoever is not from God does not listen to us. This is how we recognise the Spirit of truth and the spirit of falsehood.

For worship. Thank God for the apostolic word preserved in Scripture. Listen to it as the voice of truth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — God Is Love: The Source, the Measure, and the Goal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “God is love.” John does not mean a warm feeling or a tolerant mood. Love is the life the Father, Son and Spirit have shared from eternity. And this love has been shown: God sent his only Son so that we might live through him, as the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we ought to love one another. And when we do, the invisible God is seen in his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Love

Love is from God, and God showed it by sending his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The departing teachers’ knowledge produced schism, not love.

Now: No one has ever seen God; when we love one another, his love is made complete in us.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.

Beloved, let us love one another. Key words. “Beloved” (agapētoi, loved ones). Those who are loved should love.

For love is from God. Key words. “From God” (ek tou theou): love has its source in God. All genuine love flows from him.

And whoever loves has been born of God and knows God. Key words. “Loves” (agapōn, present tense: habitually loves, with agapē, self-giving love). “Has been born of God” (ek tou theou gegennētai, perfect tense). Love is evidence of the new birth. “Knows God” (ginōskei ton theon). Those who love show they know God, because they share his nature.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who shows any kind of love is born again. John means agape love, the self-giving love defined by the cross (v. 10; 3:16), flowing from faith in Christ (v. 15). Many unbelievers show natural affection and kindness, by God’s common grace, but not the love that comes from new birth.

In a sentence. Dear friends, let us love one another, for love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.

On a Tuesday. Love is from God. Ask him today for more of his love, and show it to someone.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.

Anyone who does not love does not know God. Key words. “Does not know” (ouk egnō, aorist: never came to know). Lack of love shows that one has never known God.

Because God is love. Key words. “God is love” (ho theos agapē estin). One of the greatest statements in Scripture. Not merely that God loves, or that love is one of his attributes, but that love is his very nature. Within the Trinity, the Father, Son and Spirit have eternally loved one another (John 17:24). God did not need to create in order to love; he is love in himself. All his actions are loving, including his holiness and justice. As God is light (1:5), so God is love. The two go together: his love is holy, and his holiness is loving.

Where Christians differ: if God is love, can he send anyone to hell? Some argue that a God of love could never punish anyone eternally, and so all will be saved, or the wicked will be annihilated. Verdict: “God is love” does not mean love is God, or that God’s love overrides his holiness and justice. The same John who wrote “God is love” wrote that the wrath of God remains on those who reject the Son (John 3:36) and described the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10–15). God’s love is seen supremely at the cross, where he satisfied his own justice by bearing his own wrath in his Son (v. 10). Love that ignores evil would not be true love. God is love, and God is light; his love is holy love. Those who reject his love in Christ face his just and eternal judgement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is soft, permissive or indulgent. True love seeks the highest good of the beloved, and sometimes that means discipline (Hebrews 12:6) and justice.

In a sentence. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.

For worship. Worship the God who is love: Father, Son and Spirit, eternally loving, and loving you.

verseByVerse.quote: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.

In this the love of God was made manifest among us. Key words. “Made manifest” (ephanerōthē, revealed, shown, made visible). God’s love is not just a feeling; it became visible in an event.

That God sent his only Son into the world. Key words. “Sent” (apestalken, perfect tense: sent, with continuing effects). “Only Son” (monogenē, unique, one of a kind, only begotten), as in John 1:14, 18; 3:16. The Son is unique; no other is Son as he is. The Father gave what was most precious to him (Romans 8:32; Genesis 22:2).

So that we might live through him. Key words. “Live” (zēsōmen): eternal life, now and forever (John 3:16; 10:10). “Through him” (di’ autou): Christ is the means and source of life. We were spiritually dead (3:14); through him we live.

What it does not mean. “Only Son” does not mean the Son was created or had a beginning. “Only begotten” expresses his unique, eternal relationship with the Father, not a beginning in time.

In a sentence. This is how God showed his love among us: he sent his one and only Son into the world so that we might live through him.

For worship. Thank the Father for sending his only Son, so that you might live through him.

verseByVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.

In this is love. Key words. The definition of love.

Not that we have loved God. Key words. Love did not begin with us. We did not seek God; we were his enemies (Romans 3:11; 5:10). Our love for God is always a response, never the origin.

But that he loved us. Key words. “He loved” (ēgapēsen, aorist: a decisive act). God took the initiative, when we were unlovable (Romans 5:8; Ephesians 2:4–5).

And sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Key words. “Propitiation” (hilasmon), as in 2:2: the sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath by bearing it in our place. The supreme expression of God’s love is that he himself provided the sacrifice to satisfy his own justice (Romans 3:25–26). This is not an angry Father appeased by a loving Son; it is the loving Father sending his Son to bear the wrath that sin deserves. Love and justice meet at the cross. Penal substitution is the heart of God’s love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s love is opposed to his wrath. His love is shown precisely in dealing with his wrath against sin by bearing it himself in his Son.

In a sentence. This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath from our sins.

For worship. Meditate on this definition of love today. You did not love him first; he loved you, and sent his Son to bear your punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.

Beloved, if God so loved us. Key words. “If” (ei): since. “So” (houtōs, in this way, to this extent): in the way just described, sending his Son as a propitiation (v. 10). Echoing John 3:16.

We also ought to love one another. Key words. “Ought” (opheilomen, owe, are obligated), as in 3:16. We owe love to others because of the love God has shown us. Not to repay God (we never could), but to pass his love on. Those who have received such love cannot withhold it from others (Matthew 18:21–35).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we love others only out of duty. The love of God poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5) becomes the source and motive of our love.

In a sentence. Dear friends, since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.

On a Tuesday. Think of the hardest person in your church to love. God loved you when you were hard to love. Love them this week.

verseByVerse.quote: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.

No one has ever seen God. Key words. “Seen” (tetheatai, beheld, gazed upon, perfect tense). The same statement as John 1:18. God in his essence is invisible (1 Timothy 6:16). The false teachers may have claimed special visions of God.

If we love one another, God abides in us. Key words. Though God is invisible, he becomes visible through his people’s love. When believers love one another, God’s presence among them is evident (John 13:35). The invisible God is seen in the love of his children.

And his love is perfected in us. Key words. “Perfected” (teteleiōmenē, completed, brought to its goal, perfect tense), as in 2:5. God’s love for us reaches its intended goal when it produces love in us for others. God’s love is not complete until it flows through us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God abides in us only because we love. God abides in us by his Spirit, given at new birth (v. 13). Our love is the evidence of his presence.

In a sentence. No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God lives in us and his love is made complete in us.

For worship. Ask God to make his invisible love visible through you today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Abiding in Love: Confidence, Fear Cast Out, and the Visible Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Assurance rests on the Spirit God has given (v. 13) and the confession of his Son (v. 15). From that union comes confidence even for the day of judgment, because “as he is so also are we in this world.” Perfect love casts out the fear of punishment. And love for the invisible God is tested by love for the brother we can see.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear Cast Out

Those who abide in love have confidence for the day of judgement. Perfect love casts out fear, and we love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Confidence rested on union with the Son, not on claimed knowledge.

Now: The brother we can see tests our love for the God we cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.

By this we know that we abide in him and he in us. Key words. Mutual indwelling, as in 3:24.

Because he has given us of his Spirit. Key words. “Of his Spirit” (ek tou pneumatos autou, from his Spirit). Every believer has received the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:9). The Spirit is God’s pledge that we belong to him (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13–14). His presence is known by his work: enabling us to confess Christ (v. 2), to love (vv. 7, 12), and to cry out to God as Abba, Father (Romans 8:15–16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we receive only part of the Spirit. “Of his Spirit” means we share in the Spirit God gives. He is a person, not a substance divided up.

In a sentence. This is how we know that we live in him and he in us: he has given us of his Spirit.

For worship. Thank God for his Spirit within you, the pledge that you belong to him forever.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.

And we have seen and testify. Key words. “We”: the apostles, eyewitnesses (1:1–3). “Seen” (tetheametha, beheld, perfect tense). Though no one has seen God (v. 12), the apostles saw the Son, who reveals the Father (John 1:18; 14:9).
