That the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world. Key words. “Savior of the world” (sōtēra tou kosmou): the title the Samaritans gave Jesus (John 4:42). Not just the Saviour of Jews, but of people from every nation. In the Roman world, the emperor was hailed as “saviour of the world”; John gives the title to its true owner.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in the world will be saved. Jesus is the Saviour of the world in that he is the only Saviour for all peoples, and he saves people from every nation (Revelation 5:9). Those who reject him are not saved (John 3:18, 36).

In a sentence. And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Saviour of the world.

For worship. Praise Jesus, the Saviour of the world. Pray for a nation or people group that needs to hear of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.

Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God. Key words. “Confesses” (homologēsē, acknowledges, declares). The true confession, which the false teachers denied (2:22–23; 4:2–3). Not merely words, but genuine faith that Jesus, the man, is the eternal Son of God.

God abides in him, and he in God. Key words. Mutual indwelling. Confession of Christ is evidence of union with God. Faith, love and the Spirit all bear witness together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that merely reciting a creed brings union with God. The confession must come from genuine faith (Romans 10:9–10), and it will be accompanied by love (v. 16).

In a sentence. If anyone acknowledges that Jesus is the Son of God, God lives in them and they in God.

For worship. Confess today, aloud: Jesus is the Son of God. And rejoice that God lives in you.

verseByVerse.quote: So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.

So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. Key words. “Come to know” (egnōkamen) and “believe” (pepisteukamen), both perfect tense: we have known and believed, and continue to. Knowing and believing God’s love go together. We know it because he has shown it (vv. 9–10); we believe it by faith. “Has for us” (echei en hēmin, has in us, among us).

God is love. Key words. Repeated from verse 8 for emphasis.

And whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him. Key words. “Abides in love” (menōn en tē agapē): lives continually in God’s love, receiving it and showing it. To live in love is to live in God, because God is love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who loves anything is in God. The love in view is God’s love revealed in Christ, received by faith (v. 15).

In a sentence. And so we know and rely on the love God has for us. God is love. Whoever lives in love lives in God, and God in them.

For worship. Rest in God’s love for you today. Know it, believe it, and live in it.

verseByVerse.quote: By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.

By this is love perfected with us. Key words. “By this”: by abiding in love (v. 16). “Perfected” (teteleiōtai, brought to completion).

So that we may have confidence for the day of judgment. Key words. “Confidence” (parrēsian, boldness), as in 2:28 and 3:21. “Day of judgment” (tē hēmera tēs kriseōs): the final judgement at Christ’s return. Believers can face it without fear.

Because as he is so also are we in this world. Key words. “As he is”: Christ, now exalted, perfectly loved by the Father and righteous. “So also are we”: we share his standing before the Father. We are loved as he is loved (John 17:23), accepted in him, righteous in him. And we are being made like him in love. Because we are in him, the judgement holds no terror (Romans 8:1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are as perfect as Christ in character now. It means they share his acceptance and standing with the Father, and are growing in his likeness.

In a sentence. This is how love is made complete among us, so that we will have confidence on the day of judgement: in this world we are like Jesus.

For worship. Thank God that because you are in Christ, you can face the day of judgement with confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.

There is no fear in love. Key words. “Fear” (phobos): here, terror, dread of punishment. Not the reverent fear of God that Scripture commends (Proverbs 1:7; 1 Peter 1:17), but the terrified dread of a criminal before a judge.

But perfect love casts out fear. Key words. “Perfect love” (hē teleia agapē, complete, mature love). “Casts out” (exō ballei, throws out, drives away). As we grow in knowing God’s love for us, terror is driven out. Love and terror cannot coexist.

For fear has to do with punishment. Key words. “Punishment” (kolasin, penalty, correction). Fear expects punishment. But for believers, Christ has borne the punishment (v. 10). There is nothing left to fear.

And whoever fears has not been perfected in love. Key words. Fear of judgement shows that God’s love has not yet fully penetrated the heart. The cure is to know and believe his love more deeply (v. 16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should never feel any fear, or that reverent fear of God is wrong. It means terror of condemnation has no place in those who know God’s love in Christ (Romans 8:15).

In a sentence. There is no fear in love. But perfect love drives out fear, because fear has to do with punishment. The one who fears is not made perfect in love.

For worship. If you fear God’s judgement, look again at the cross: your punishment has been borne. Let his love drive out your fear.

verseByVerse.quote: We love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We love because he first loved us.

We love because he first loved us. Key words. “We love” (hēmeis agapōmen): either a statement (we love) or an exhortation (let us love). Probably a statement. “Because” (hoti). “First” (prōtos): God’s love came first, before we loved him or anyone (v. 10). Our love is always a response to his. Some manuscripts add “him” (we love him); others “God.” Most likely the original simply says “we love,” covering love for God and for others. God’s love is the source, cause and pattern of all our love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we loved God before he drew us. Our love is entirely his gift and work in us (Romans 5:5). This is grace: God loves first, and his love produces ours.

In a sentence. We love because he first loved us.

For worship. Memorise this verse. Let it humble you and fill you with gratitude: he loved you first.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.

If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. Key words. Another false claim, as in 1:6, 8, 10; 2:4, 6, 9. “Liar” (pseustēs). A claim to love God while hating a fellow believer is false.

For he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen. Key words. “Has seen” (heōraken). An argument from easier to harder: if you cannot love a visible person, how can you love the invisible God? Love for God is tested by love for his children, who bear his image and are his family.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love for God depends on love for people. Love for God comes first. But the two are so connected that the absence of one exposes the absence of the other.

In a sentence. Whoever claims to love God yet hates a brother or sister is a liar. For whoever does not love their brother and sister, whom they have seen, cannot love God, whom they have not seen.

On a Tuesday. Your love for God will show in how you treat his people this week. Love them practically.

verseByVerse.quote: And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.

And this commandment we have from him. Key words. “From him”: from Christ, or God.

Whoever loves God must also love his brother. Key words. “Must also” (kai, also). The two great commandments, love for God and love for neighbour, are inseparable (Mark 12:29–31). You cannot have one without the other.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love for others is equal to love for God. God is to be loved with all our heart; neighbours as ourselves. But love for God always overflows in love for others.

In a sentence. And he has given us this command: anyone who loves God must also love their brother and sister.

For worship. Ask God to deepen your love for him today, and to let it overflow to the people around you.

4.theology:
God is Love. The statement "God is love" (vv. 8, 16) is one of the most misused sentences in Scripture. It is taken to mean that love is God — that whatever we call love must be divine, that God must approve of whatever we name as love. John means the opposite: God defines love, not the other way around. And he defines it immediately by a specific act: the sending of the Son to be the propitiation. To say "God is love" in John's sense is to say that God, in his innermost being, is the kind of God who sends his only Son into the world to die for sinners who could not save themselves. That is the love John is talking about. It is not soft; it is costly. It is not tolerant; it is propitiatory. It is not vague; it has flesh and blood and a cross and an empty tomb.

The Expulsion of Fear. The pastoral application of the doctrine of propitiation in verses 17–18 is one of the most comforting passages in the New Testament. The believer who is tortured by fear of God's judgment has not yet fully grasped what the propitiation means: that the very wrath they fear has been exhausted, absorbed, satisfied in the beloved Son. Perfect love casts out fear not by denying the reality of judgment but by pointing to the one who bore it. Reformed theology speaks of the "double jeopardy" of the cross: it would be unjust for God to punish twice what Christ has already borne. The blood of Jesus is the answer to every accusing conscience, every fear of condemnation, every midnight terror of a soul that wonders whether it is safe with God.
4.examples:
Then: The community had been shaken by teachers who claimed spiritual authority and offered a more sophisticated understanding of God. The test John gives is arrestingly simple: do they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? Not "do they seem spiritual?" Not "do they have impressive experiences?" But: do they hold to the incarnation? This is always the fault line. Every theological error that has ever devastated a church has at some point compromised either the full deity or the full humanity of Christ. John's readers are given a test simple enough for a child and decisive enough to unmask every false spirit.

Now: "We love because he first loved us" is the answer to every form of Christian guilt and striving. The Christian life is not a performance of love in order to earn God's approval; it is a response of love to a love already given, already completed, already victorious at the cross. When love runs dry — as it will — the answer is not to try harder but to go back to the source: "In this is love, not that we have loved God..." The spring of all Christian love is the love of God in the cross of his Son. Drink there again, and love will flow.

5.title: Faith that Overcomes, Life that is Sure
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.<sup>2</sup>By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.<sup>3</sup>For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.<sup>4</sup>For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.<sup>5</sup>Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?<sup>6</sup>This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.<sup>7</sup>For there are three that testify:<sup>8</sup>the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.<sup>9</sup>If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.<sup>10</sup>Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.<sup>11</sup>And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.<sup>12</sup>Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.<sup>13</sup>I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.<sup>14</sup>And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.<sup>15</sup>And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.<sup>16</sup>If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that.<sup>17</sup>All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.<sup>18</sup>We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.<sup>19</sup>We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.<sup>20</sup>And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.<sup>21</sup>Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
5.overview:
The last chapter draws the letter’s threads together. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, loves God’s children and overcomes the world, and the victory is faith. God has testified about his Son, and his testimony is this: eternal life is in the Son. “Whoever has the Son has life.”

Then John states his purpose: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Not hope or feel, but know. Those who know may pray with confidence and intercede for a sinning brother. The letter ends with Jesus Christ declared “the true God and eternal life”, and one last command: keep yourselves from idols.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Faith, Love, and the World-Overcoming Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John ties faith, new birth and love together as a single reality. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Messiah has been born of God, and anyone who loves the Father loves his children too. We know we love God’s children when we love God and keep his commands, and his commands are not a crushing weight. For everyone born of God overcomes the world, and the victory that overcomes the world is our faith. Who overcomes the world? Only the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as the Victory

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God and loves God’s children. Faith in the Son of God overcomes the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ordinary faith in Jesus was being called insufficient.

Now: The faith that overcomes is not heroic; it is trust in the Son of God who has already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and loves God’s other children.

Birth and faith. The Greek tense says the believer “has been born” of God. New birth is the source of faith, and faith is the evidence of new birth. This is a strong text for the Reformed teaching that regeneration comes before, and produces, faith (John 1:12–13).

Family love. If you love the Father, you will love his children. Love for the head of the family reaches the whole family.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know we love God’s children when we love God and keep his commands.

Two directions. In 4:20, love for the visible brother tested love for God. Here love for God tests love for the brother. They are not in tension. True love for others is shaped by obedience to God, and obedience to God includes loving others. Love that ignores God’s commands is not love for his children.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for God is keeping his commands, which are not burdensome.

Not burdensome. The word means heavy or crushing. For those born of God, his law is not an outside weight but the expression of a new heart that delights in his will (Psalm 119:35).

What it does not mean. It does not mean obedience is never hard. Christ called us to take up a cross. It means God’s commands are not a crushing yoke, because he gives the love and strength to keep them (Matthew 11:30).

On a Tuesday. If obeying God feels like nothing but a grind, the answer is not only to try harder. Ask whether you have stopped looking at his love. Return to the cross, and the commands will feel more like a path home than a weight.

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone born of God overcomes the world, and faith is the victory.

Already won. Christ said, “I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Faith is the hand that holds on to the one who has already won, and so shares his victory.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God overcomes the world.

Faith in this person. Not general spirituality or self-belief, but faith in Jesus as God’s Son. The question shuts out every other way, and opens the door to anyone who believes.

On a Tuesday. A young Christian at university feels outnumbered and outargued. She does not overcome the world by winning every debate, but by trusting the Son of God, who has already overcome it. That frees her to speak with courage and kindness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Three Witnesses and the Life That Is in the Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under Jewish law a matter was settled by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides three: the Spirit, the water and the blood. The water and blood mark the beginning and end of Jesus’ ministry, his baptism and his death. God’s own testimony is greater than any human testimony, and it is this: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. There is no middle ground: whoever has the Son has life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Three Witnesses

The Spirit, the water and the blood agree: the one who was baptised is the one who died. God has given eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teaching separated the Christ of the baptism from the Jesus of the cross.

Now: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus Christ came by water and blood, his baptism and his death, and the Spirit testifies.

What water and blood mean. Some take them as the water and blood from Jesus’ side (John 19:34); others as baptism and the Lord’s Supper. The most likely reading is Jesus’ baptism, where his ministry began, and his death, where it was completed. The false teachers said the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and left before the cross. John insists that the same Son of God was baptised and crucified: “not by the water only but by the water and the blood.”

Why it matters. If only a man died on the cross, there is no atonement. The Son of God himself shed his blood.
verseByVerse.note: “Water and blood” probably refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death — against teachers who said the divine Christ left Jesus before the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are three that testify: the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit, the water and the blood agree in their testimony.

Enough testimony. Three witnesses speak with one voice about Jesus. Those who deny him do not lack evidence.

A textual note. The King James Version adds words here about the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost bearing witness in heaven, “and these three are one”. This addition, known as the Johannine Comma, is missing from almost every Greek manuscript before the sixteenth century and appears first in late Latin copies, apparently as a marginal comment. It is almost certainly not original. Nothing is lost: the Trinity is taught throughout Scripture and never depended on this line.
verseByVerse.note: Some late manuscripts add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven (known from the King James Version). They are not in the early Greek manuscripts and the ESV omits them.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s testimony about his Son is greater than any human testimony.

From lesser to greater. We trust human witnesses every day, in courts, history books and doctors’ reports. God cannot lie. He has testified about his Son at his baptism (Matthew 3:17), by raising him from the dead (Romans 1:4) and by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To refuse God’s testimony is to make him a liar.

Inner witness. The Spirit confirms in the believer what the apostles proclaimed (Romans 8:16).

Unbelief is not neutral. To hear God’s clear testimony and refuse it is to call him a liar. Unbelief is not simply lack of information; it is a refusal to trust God.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s testimony is that he has given us eternal life in his Son.

A gift in a person. Eternal life is given, already, to be received. And it is found in the Son, not apart from him. No ritual or effort can give life outside Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life.

No middle ground. Life is not a matter of degrees here. The Son is either received by faith or not. This is the widest invitation (anyone may have the Son) and the narrowest claim (there is no other way to life).

On a Tuesday. A kind, moral neighbour says she has no need of Jesus. It feels harsh to say she lacks life. But love tells the truth gently, and offers the Son, in whom life is freely given.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Knowing What We Have in Christ: Assurance, Prayer, and the True God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John states his purpose: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Those who know may pray boldly, intercede for a brother who sins, and rest in three great certainties: the one born of God is kept from the evil one; we belong to God while the world lies in the power of the evil one; and the Son of God has come and given us understanding to know the true God. He is “the true God and eternal life”. So keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.theology:
That You May Know

John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life. They may pray with confidence, intercede for a sinning brother, and rest in what they know.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The letter closes on Jesus Christ as the true God and eternal life.

Now: Having the true God, refuse every substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John writes so that believers may know that they have eternal life.

Know. Not hope, guess or feel on good days, but know. Assurance is not arrogance. It is the right response to the reliability of God’s word about his Son.

The tests and assurance. John’s tests of belief, obedience and love are not meant to make sincere believers anxious, but to give them certainty. They also expose false confidence.

On a Tuesday. A Christian is asked, “Are you sure you will go to heaven?” She hesitates, afraid of sounding proud. She can answer humbly, “Yes, not because I am good, but because God has given me life in his Son, and he does not lie.”
verseByVerse.note: John’s Gospel was written that readers might believe; this letter that believers might know they have eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We can be confident that God hears whatever we ask according to his will.

According to his will. This is not a limit that lowers expectations, but a promise: prayer that matches God’s will is always heard. It turns prayer from anxious pleading into confident alignment with what God is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he hears us, we have what we ask.

“We have”. Not “we will have”. God’s hearing is as good as his giving, even before we see the answer.

What it does not mean. It is not a blank cheque for any wish called prayer. It is the confidence of someone whose asking has been shaped by God’s will and word.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers should pray for a brother whose sin is not unto death.

What is the “sin leading to death”? Three main views. Some see the unforgivable sin of blasphemy against the Spirit (Matthew 12:31–32). Some see sin that brings physical death as God’s discipline, as with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11). The most likely view, in the context of this letter, is settled, unrepentant denial of Christ by those who have left the church (2:19, 22). We should not be dogmatic.

What it does not mean. John does not forbid prayer for anyone. He simply does not command it in that case. And he does not mean a Christian who has fallen badly is beyond hope; his main point is the opposite: pray, and God gives life.

On a Tuesday. You learn that a church friend has fallen into serious sin. The temptation is to gossip or to give up on him. John says: pray for him, by name, and go to him gently. God gives life through the prayers of his people.
verseByVerse.note: The “sin that leads to death” is probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by those who left the church.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those born of God do not keep on sinning, for the Son of God keeps them.

Who protects? “He who was born of God” is almost certainly Christ, the unique Son, who keeps his own (John 10:28; 17:12). Some manuscripts read “keeps himself”, but the reading the ESV follows, that Christ keeps him, fits the context and has strong support.

What it does not mean. It is not a promise of freedom from temptation or attack. It means the evil one cannot lay hold of the believer to destroy him. The Christian is not untouched by battle, but cannot be finally defeated.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We belong to God, while the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.

Two domains. The world “lies” in the evil one’s power, like someone asleep in an enemy’s arms, unaware. Believers live in hostile territory, but belong to God, kept by the one in them who is greater (4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God has come and given us understanding to know the true God; he is the true God and eternal life.

The circle closes. The letter began with the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared (1:2). It ends by declaring that this life is Jesus Christ himself.

“He is the true God.” Some think “he” refers to the Father. But the nearest person named is Jesus Christ, and John has just called him “eternal life” (1:2; 5:11). This is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s deity in the New Testament.

For worship. The Christian does not merely know about God. Through the Son, we know him, and we are in him. That is the end of all theology: adoration.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

An abrupt, fitting end. In Ephesus, real idols filled the streets. But an idol is anything that takes the place of the true God: a false picture of Christ, a love that rules the heart, a teacher who offers less than “the true God and eternal life”.

The best protection. Not anxious watchfulness alone, but deep delight in the one who is true. Those who treasure the real are less easily fooled by counterfeits.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you turn to when you are anxious, bored or hurt: your phone, food, work, someone’s approval. Name it, turn back to Christ, and tell him he is better.

5.theology:
Faith as Victory. The declaration of 5:4 — "this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith" — is one of the most important statements about the nature of faith in Scripture. Faith is not a spiritual achievement, a heightened state of consciousness, or a moral virtue we cultivate. It is a hand that receives, a trust that rests, a confidence that looks away from itself to the Son of God who has already overcome. "Has overcome" — this points to the finished work of Christ at the cross as the source and ground of the believer's victory. We do not overcome the world by spiritual heroism; we overcome it by trusting the one who already has.

Assurance as Gift. The stated purpose of the letter — "that you may know that you have eternal life" (5:13) — stands as a rebuke to every theology that treats Christian assurance as presumption or spiritual pride. John writes to produce certainty. Reformed theology has always distinguished between assurance and presumption: presumption claims safety without evidence; assurance rests on the testimony of the Spirit, the evidence of new birth, and the promises of God. The three tests of the letter are not meant to produce anxiety but confirmation — the gentle hand of a faithful pastor showing the believer where the signs of life are visible. To know that you have eternal life is not arrogance; it is the appropriate response to the faithfulness of the God who cannot lie.
5.examples:
Then: The community, battered by false teaching and painful departure, needed to know one thing above all: that they had not missed it, that they were in the Son, that the life they had received was real and was eternal. John writes to give them that certainty — not a new experience, not a higher spirituality, but the settled confidence of those who have the Son and therefore have life. The simplicity of the final verdict — "whoever has the Son has life" — is both the most inclusive and most exclusive statement possible: inclusive, because anyone may have the Son; exclusive, because there is no life outside of him.

Now: In an age of therapeutic Christianity, where the goal is often feeling good about ourselves, John's letter is a corrective and a comfort. Assurance in John is not a feeling to be cultivated; it is a knowledge to be received — grounded in the testimony of God himself (5:9–10), confirmed by the evidence of new birth, and resting ultimately on the person of the Son. "This is the true God and eternal life" — Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever. Whatever else may be uncertain in a Christian life, this is not: whoever has the Son has life, and the Son cannot be taken away.
